subject: ANTH
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (ANTH 2302) Introduction to Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the basic principles of studying past human cultures through material remains. Surveys the fundamentals of archaeological practice and frameworks, applying interdisciplinary methods to reconstruct and interpret the archaeological record. Engages with written, oral and visual communication of archaeological data. Develops an understanding of how cultures adapt and change through time and across space. Engages critical thinking skills in evaluation of evidence and synthesis of different types of information. Introduces careers in anthropology and archaeology and the skills needed for them. TOPICS AND THEMES. Interdisciplinary nature of archaeological research. Site formation, survival and identification. Field and laboratory methods including survey, excavation, recording, curation and various types of analysis including dating methods. Relationships between humans and environments. Human evolution and behavior including past movement, subsistence strategies, foraging strategies, trade, tool production and development, sedentism, symbolic and ritual behaviors, domestication, city and state formation and reconstruction of past social and individual identities. Archaeological ethics, the role of archaeology in contemporary society and heritage management. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (ANTH 2351) Social and Cultural Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides overview of the field of social and cultural anthropology, exploring the diverse ways that human cultures shape experience across the globe, and the anthropological theory and research that attempt to understand this process. Through an exploration of different cultures, examines the major dimensions of cultural variation, including subsistence, family structure, political systems, language, religion and more. Fosters critical evaluation of cultural theories and different perspectives while promoting respectful discussion of complex and provocative topics. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Key themes include culture, ethnographic methodology and the tension between relativist and universalist perspectives. Additional topics include kinship, family structure, gender, religion, language, subsistence, political systems, race, colonialism and applied anthropology; also taught at Galveston campus.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Anthropology of Religion. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Applies fundamental principles of cultural anthropology (the study of human variation and commonalities using a holistic mindset) to the analysis of religion. Examines the relationships connecting religion, culture, society and the individual through cross-cultural, theoretical analysis of religion as a cultural phenomenon. Investigates core questions regarding the existence and persistence of religion, analyzing how religious behavior manifests and connects with other cultural elements across diverse global settings. Develops skills to critically assess research findings, analyze differing viewpoints and perspectives and formulate hypothetical research agendas. Engages potentially charged topics in diverse settings, challenging students to explore their own assumptions and biases regarding their personal worldview. Fosters greater understanding of self-awareness and personal responsibility in society through exploration of the diversity of religious behaviors. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers theoretical approaches to the study of religion; analyzes religious features including symbolism, myth and ritual; studies religious specialists, magic, divination and witchcraft; explores altered states of consciousness; evaluates beliefs regarding gods, spirits, souls, ghosts and death; assesses religious change and searches for new meaning; examines religious violence and fundamentalism; and investigates vernacular religion, secularism, atheism and irreligion. Includes analysis of religious practices, beliefs and institutions from a variety of cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus. Cross-listed with RELS 403.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (SPCH 1315) Public Speaking. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles, practice and criticism of public speaking. Emphasizes public speaking as more than performance, examining key skills, including audience analysis, research, organization, use of supporting materials and delivery techniques. Attention to ethical communication and sensitivity to diverse audiences across professional, political, religious, cultural and ideological contexts. Includes practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking, developing verbal and nonverbal communication strategies. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with skills essential for professional, academic and civic life. Builds competence in organizing ideas, supporting arguments, adapting them to varied audiences. Develops confidence in extemporaneous speaking, critical listening and communication across diverse contexts. Prepares students for leadership roles, workplace communication and active participation in public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about public speaking, such as viewing it only as performance or memorization, differ from research-based and practical perspectives. Develops understanding of speaking as a process involving invention, organization, style, delivery and audience adaptation, enhancing skills in extemporaneous speaking. Emphasizes that effective speaking requires ethical choices, critical thinking and sensitivity to diverse audiences as much as confidence in delivery. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of why public speaking matters in contemporary society; study of ethical principles in communication; development of confidence and listening skills; analysis of audiences and rhetorical situations; research and organization of supporting materials; crafting of effective introductions, bodies and conclusions; use of language and presentation aids; practice in informative, persuasive and ceremonial speaking; application of digital rhetoric and multimedia tools. Course speeches and examples may address diverse and sometimes controversial topics, reflecting perspectives represented in public life as well as subjects chosen by students; breadth of content emerges from student interests and experiences, and guidance from the instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication for Technical Professions. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces principles, practice and criticism of public speaking adapted for technical fields. Focus on rhetorical invention and delivery for engineers, scientists and other technical professionals who must present complex information to general audiences, policymakers and interdisciplinary teams. Emphasizes public speaking as more than performance, examining key skills including audience analysis, research, organization, use of supporting materials and delivery techniques. Special attention to clarity, analogy and visualization as tools for translating technical knowledge. Includes practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking while integrating visual and graphic materials into their presentations. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with communication skills essential for technical professions. Builds competence in simplifying complex information, supporting arguments with evidence and adapting content for non-experts. Develops confidence in delivering technical presentations in professional, academic and civic settings. Prepares students for roles requiring leadership, interdisciplinary collaboration and the ability to explain technical processes to decision-makers and the public. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ways of describing technical work may not be effective outside specialized fields. Develops understanding of ways technical communication techniques—such as analogy, narrative and visualization—shape audience comprehension and trust. Emphasizes that effective technical communication requires ethical choices, critical thinking and sensitivity to diverse audiences as much as subject matter expertise. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of why communication matters in technical professions; study of ethical principles in technical communication; development of confidence and listening skills; analysis of general and specialized audiences; research and organization of technical content; crafting of effective introductions, bodies and conclusions; use of analogies, language and presentation aids to explain complex information; practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking; integration of visual and graphic materials into technical presentations. prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 304 and junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Mechanics of Advanced Aerospace Structures. (3-0). Credit 3. Advanced analysis techniques for aerospace structures; material anisotropy, plasticity, fatigue and fracture; laminated materials; solution of plane elasticity, plate and multi-component structural configurations; buckling of beams and plates; application of finite element analysis. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AERO 304 and junior or senior classification.

subject: AERO
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 304.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Aerospace Materials Science. (3-0). Credit 3. Relationship between aerospace engineering material properties and microstructure; mechanical and thermal properties; environmental degradation; mechanical failure. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in AERO 304.

subject: AERO
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 303 and AERO 351.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Computational Fluid Dynamics for Aerospace Applications. (3-0). Credit 3. Present methods for solving internal and external flow problems for inviscid and viscous compressible flow; Euler, Navier-Stokes and Large Eddy Simulation solvers, boundary conditions formulation, and basics of parallel processing. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in AERO 303 and AERO 351.

subject: AERO
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 321; grade C or better in AERO 401, or concurrent enrollment.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Aircraft Design. (3-0). Credit 3. There are three major phases of aircraft design: (1) conceptual design, (2) preliminary design and (3) detail design. The aircraft design process starts with identifying requirements and performing initial calculations to generate the overall concept of the aircraft. In preliminary design, we design the aircraft’s systems and subsystems. Finally, in detail design, we specify how the aircraft will be fabricated and tested. The course introduces students to tools and methods used in the conceptual and preliminary design of fixed-wing aircraft. Students will learn about aircraft design requirements, aircraft mission, weight estimation, aerodynamics and propulsion analysis, performance analysis, stability characteristics and cost estimation. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AERO 321; grade C or better in AERO 401, or concurrent enrollment.

subject: AERO
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 351.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Aerospace Propulsion. (3-0). Credit 3. Air breathing propulsion; design and analysis of inlets, compressors, combustors, turbines and nozzles; application to aeronautical, aerospace, ground transportation and energy. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in AERO 351.

prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 321.

Introduction to the Theory of Automatic Control specifically applied to aerospace vehicles; techniques for analysis and synthesis of linear control systems, stability criteria, systems response and performance criteria; design studies of active controls to improve aerospace vehicle performance. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in AERO 321.

prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 222 or MATH 417.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Numerical Simulation. (3-0). Credit 3. Numerical and analytical simulation of physical problems in sciences and engineering using applied methods; developing and using numerical techniques for physical problems described by nonlinear algebraic equations, ordinary and partial differential equations. Prerequisite:Grade of C or better in AERO 222 or MATH 417.

subject: AERO
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 303.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Aerothermochemistry. (3-0). Credit 3. Composition of chemically reacting gases (air and propellant); thermodynamic functions based on classical and quantum mechanical theories; calculation of gas temperatures; equilibrium, frozen and non-equilibrium flows through nozzles and shock waves. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in AERO 303.

subject: AERO
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Human Factors Engineering for Aerospace Designs. (3-0). Credit 3. Physiological and psychophysiological issues encountered in aviation and space environments and their effect on human cognitive and physical performance; survey methods for human workload and performance evaluations; apply human-systems design principles to an aerospace design project. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with ISEN 432.

subject: AERO
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 321.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Machine Learning for Aerospace Engineers. (3-0). Credit 3. This course discusses fundamental concepts and algorithms in machine learning with a focus on aerospace applications. Students will learn to model, analyze and interpret data arising from flight dynamics, aerodynamics and space systems. The course emphasizes both theoretical understanding and practical implementation using aerospace datasets. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AERO 321.

subject: AERO
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AERO 310 or equivalent; senior classification.

Applying this knowledge produces more informed citizens, who are proficient in the abilities required by today’s workforce. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. subject: AFST
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication and Black Freedom Dreams. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how Black freedom has been expressed across art, speech, political action, media, visual cultures and writings designed to challenge injustice, build solidarity and imagine alternative futures. Considers both well-known and lesser-known figures, recognizing that activism operates through leaders, communities and collective voices. Course content may include material involving racial conflict, oppression and struggle in the United States and/or around the globe. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds recognition of communication as a tool for social response, institutional critique and public engagement. Provides perspective for professional fields that require cultural awareness, ethical judgment and responsiveness to diverse audiences, such as education, media, public service, community leadership, law and advocacy-related work. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in rhetoric, media, history, social movements or communication. Contributes to civic understanding by tracing how ideas become actions through communication practices. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how articulations of Black freedom have long served as catalysts for action, social change and public debate in the United States and across the globe. Positions their strategies, not only as expressions of a specific community, but as case studies in persuasion, resistance, leadership and/or collective voice that have shaped constitutional interpretation, civic participation and public opinion more broadly. Considers how struggles for justice by one group reveal broader questions shared across groups, such as rights, authority, belonging and national identity. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of abolitionist writings, protest speeches, spirituals and freedom songs; rhetorical strategies of civil rights, Black Power and/or contemporary justice movements; analysis of communication through sermons, manifestos, poetry, performance and/or media; exploration of visual and digital media as tools of resistance and community-building; consideration of leadership, collective action and messaging in local and/or global liberation struggles. Course material may reference conflict, repression or political controversy as relevant to understanding communication within movements for freedom and justice. Course content is selected to align with the course description and the current state of scholarship in the field. Instructors who teach this class may assign different readings and/or course topics that fit within the course description and meet the learning objectives. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with COMM 425.

prerequisite_text: ECON 323 or equivalent, or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Food Security, Climate and Conflict. (3-0). Credit 3. prerequisite_text: AGEC 621 or equivalent.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Data Science in Applied Agribusiness. (3-0). Credit 3. Regression based causal models are limited in their capacity in identifying causal inference patterns among set of variables in complex agribusiness systems where multitude of variables interact. A vast majority of work in data science in agribusiness encompasses the use of observational data in modeling and forecasting decision-making variables. Prerequisites: AGEC 621 or equivalent.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Visualizing and Understanding Data with Modern Tools. Credit 1 to 4. This course provides an advanced, application-oriented exploration of modern analytics techniques used in business research and decision making. Students will move beyond foundational regression into advanced modeling approaches, including regularization, count models, Bayesian regression, time-series forecasting, causal analysis, machine learning algorithms, AI/NLP and neural networks. The course integrates statistical rigor with hands-on implementation in R and SAS, followed by visualization and dashboard development using Tableau. Through data cases, quizzes, assignments and a capstone presentation, students will learn to translate complex analytical outputs into strategic business insights. By the end of the semester, students will be able to build, evaluate, interpret and communicate advanced predictive and causal models for real-world business problems. Prerequisites: Enrollment in Masters of Science in Analytics Program.

Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in ANSC 111, ANSC 113 and ANSC 303; junior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Animal Feeds and Feeding. (2-3). Credit 3. Scientific approaches associated with precision feeding and diet formulation to match nutrient availabilities of feedstuffs with requirements of various classes of livestock species; emphasis on cost-effective feeding strategies to optimize animal productivity, and end-product quality and safety, while mitigating environmental impacts and enhancing animal health and welfare. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ANSC 111, ANSC 113 and ANSC 303; junior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: BICH 410 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Physiology and Biochemistry of Muscle as a Food. (3-0). Credit 3. Biochemical, histological, anatomical and physical characteristics of muscle cells and factors associated with transformation of muscle cells into meat. Prerequisite: BICH 410 or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with FSTC 607.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: ANSC 406 or ANSC 408.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Beef Cattle Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Current knowledge of beef cattle ranch and feedlot production systems; nutrition, management, breeding, body composition, economics, health, pollution and sanitation control. Prerequisite: ANSC 406 or ANSC 408.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: BICH 411 or BICH 601 or equivalent or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Protein Metabolism. (3-0). Credit 3. Basic concepts and recent advances in protein metabolism in animals with emphasis on physiological and nutritional significances; discussion of protein digestion; absorption of peptides; absorption, synthesis and degradation of amino acids; hormonal and nutritional regulation of protein turnover; determination of protein quality and requirements. Prerequisite: BICH 411 or BICH 601 or equivalent or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with NUTR 613.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: Approval of instructor or enrollment in master of equine industry management program.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Issues in the Equine Industry. (1-0). Credit 1. Integration of cumulative knowledge acquired in the equine science curriculum to demonstrate critical thinking and communication skills to address critical issues in the equine industry. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor or enrollment in master of equine industry management program.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Carcass Composition and Quality. (3-0). Credit 3. Survey of scientific literature regarding carcass composition; quality and palatability of meat animals; factors that affect differences among animals of the same specie; impact on value and usefulness. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: GENE 603 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Applied Animal Genomics. (3-0). Credit 3. Theory and application of genomics by livestock industries; consideration of genetic markers, gene mapping methods, genome analysis and emerging technologies such as microarrays, transgenesis, cloning and marker assisted selection; exposure to bioinformatic tools for genomics. Prerequisite: GENE 603 or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with GENE 629 and POSC 630.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Livestock and Mammalian Epigenetics. (1-0). Credit 1. Advanced instruction in the role of epigenetic regulation in mammalian species, with an emphasis on livestock; examination of how basic epigenetic mechanisms regulate gene expression and influence organismal development, disease, inter- and transgenerational inheritance in livestock; exploration of effect of environment on epigenetics in livestock; discussion of primary journal articles surveying current topics and methodologies in epigenetics. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Current Issues in Animal Agriculture. (3-0). Credit 3. Projecting a professional image and utilizing communication skills to describe animal agriculture; strengths and weaknesses of animal agriculture. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: Approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Industrial Processed Meat Operations. (2-2). Credit 3. Application of scientific principles and business practices to manufactured meat products; interrelationships among marketing, manufacturing, product development, regulatory compliance and quality assurance in commercial processed meat operations. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor. Cross-listed with FSTC 667.

subject: ANSC
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification in animal science.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Seminar. Credit 1 each semester. Important current developments in field of animal science; review of current literature and presentation of papers on selected animal science topics. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in animal science.

subject: ANSC

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (ANTH 2346, HUMA 2323) Introduction to Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Investigates anthropology as the holistic and relativistic study of humankind, exploring human life across diverse cultures, time periods and geographical locations. Examines the discipline through its four major subfields: archaeology (the study of material culture and the past), biological anthropology (the study of human evolution and variation), sociocultural anthropology (the study of cultural systems and social organization) and linguistic anthropology (the study of language construction and symbolism). Applies fundamental concepts, including the scientific method and evolutionary theory, to complex human experiences. Develops abilities in critical thinking, analysis of empirical data and effective communication, engaging with culturally diverse and sometimes controversial subjects. Analyzes the discipline’s relationship with society and its impact on global communities over time. TOPICS AND THEMES. Explores human evolutionary history, including primate behavior and hominin development; analyzes the history of human biological variation and the lack of a scientific basis for "race"; examines material culture, ancient civilizations and archaeological methods; studies language construction, symbolism and communication patterns; investigates social organization, including kinship, family, marriage and gender; explores economic systems, political structures, religion and belief systems; and applies anthropological thinking to contemporary issues such as, but not limited to, health, medicine, forensics, violence and global challenges. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world; also taught at Qatar campus.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (ANTH 2302) Introduction to Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the basic principles of studying past human cultures through material remains. Surveys the fundamentals of archaeological practice and frameworks, applying interdisciplinary methods to reconstruct and interpret the archaeological record. Engages with written, oral and visual communication of archaeological data. Develops an understanding of how cultures adapt and change through time and across space. Engages critical thinking skills in evaluation of evidence and synthesis of different types of information. Introduces careers in anthropology and archaeology and the skills needed for them. TOPICS AND THEMES. Interdisciplinary nature of archaeological research. Site formation, survival and identification. Field and laboratory methods including survey, excavation, recording, curation and various types of analysis including dating methods. Relationships between humans and environments. Human evolution and behavior including past movement, subsistence strategies, foraging strategies, trade, tool production and development, sedentism, symbolic and ritual behaviors, domestication, city and state formation and reconstruction of past social and individual identities. Archaeological ethics, the role of archaeology in contemporary society and heritage management. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology; also taught at Galveston campus.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Peoples and Cultures of the World. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys human cultures around the world using case studies of customs and cultural organization. Explores how anthropology is a holistic discipline focused on all of humanity, which integrates knowledge from diverse fields like history, economics, psychology, sociology and traditional sciences. Explores global interconnectedness alongside cultural diversity, addressing questions of "us and them". Develops a greater understanding of the breadth of variation in the human condition and the power of culture to shape individual experience. Recognizes the trade-offs between cultural relativist and universalist perspectives. Gains cultural awareness to inform future evaluations of domestic and global issues. Practices communicating opinions in a culturally respectful manner. Relates outcomes of cultural study to one’s understanding of one’s own culture. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Analyzes key anthropological concepts, including fieldwork, ethnocentrism, cultural relativism, holism and ethnography. Considers human universals and cultural uniqueness. Studies cultural expressions related to basic perceptions (color, space, distance) and the body (beauty standards, adornment, modification). Explores systems of social organization, including gender, sports, games, communication, gestures and greetings. Investigates cultural practices concerning food, eating, reciprocity, trade, etiquette, folklore and magic. Examines cultural approaches to death, dying, medicine, illness and health.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Introduction to Forensic Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examine the foundational role of forensic anthropology within the broader forensic sciences which involves analyzing human skeletal remains for medico-legal applications, covering the history of the field and its development. Build theoretical knowledge of the discipline including the history of how the discipline developed and its role in the broader forensic sciences and international, federal and state levels. Apply proper anatomical terminology, taphonomy and comparative morphological methods to discuss and describe skeletal trauma, pathologies and anomalies. Apply and practice methods used to create a "biological profile" for an individual by estimating sex, age, stature and ancestry. Consider the history and foundations of forensic anthropology; study the broader medicolegal system, professional ethics and error assessment; apply osteological methods and anatomical terminology to describing human skeletal material; describe scene recovery methods such as location, recovery and taphonomic processes; apply and critically examine methods for estimating sex, age, stature and ancestry; identify and classify infectious disease, congenital conditions and nutritional deficiencies on the skeleton and teeth; explore individual identification techniques such as facial reconstruction and genetic genealogy; critically assess how forensic anthropology is portrayed in popular culture and the media. Discuss current topics considered relevant to the field by the American Academy of Forensic Science including, but not limited to, research ethics, reassessment of biological profile estimation methods and demographic underrepresentation in comparative collections.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Historical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the material and documentary evidence of European colonization in North America and its impact on Indigenous populations, African enslaved peoples and the environment. Integrates historical records with archaeological findings to understand how European imperial powers such as the Spanish, the Basques, the French, the Dutch and the English shaped the Americas through settlement, trade and social structures. Includes case studies from contact-era settlements, plantations, forts, battlefields and maritime contexts, highlighting how artifacts, architecture and written documents complement and sometimes challenge one another. Emphasizes methods of historical archaeology, including document transcription, genealogical research, artifact analysis and field methods that provide students with tools to critically interpret North American history through a material lens. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in historical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. European exploration and colonial expansion led by European nations including Spain, Portugal, France, the Netherlands and England; Indigenous populations; forced migration and enslavement of Africans; trade, exchange and economic structures; archaeology of gender, identity, racialization, plantations, forts, battlefields, settlements, graves and shipwrecks; historical archaeological theory and methods including survey and excavation methods, absolute and relative dating methods and artifact analysis; archival and research skills including genealogical research, transcription and historical document analysis; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Nautical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines shipwrecks, sunken harbors and other submerged evidence of human activity from the Stone Age through early modern times. Explores the archaeology, technology and cultural significance of maritime societies, emphasizing the methods used to survey, map, excavate, conserve and interpret submerged sites. Reviews case examples from the Mediterranean and northern Europe, including Bronze Age, Classical, Byzantine, medieval and Viking vessels, while considering the relationship of seafaring to cultural geography and the broader human past. Ship construction, diving technology, site preservation and surveying techniques are addressed and explored through various case studies. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in nautical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Shipwrecks; submerged harbors; inundated archaeological sites; Bronze Age Mediterranean vessels; Egyptian Nile boats; Classical Greek and Phoenician ships; Greek warships (triremes, polyremes); Roman merchantmen; Byzantine ships; late medieval Mediterranean ships; late medieval warships; carracks; Scandinavian and Northern European ships; Viking ships; cogs; hulks; ship construction; rigging; armament; nautical technology; maritime trade; naval warfare; cultural geography; survey and mapping techniques; excavation and conservation methods; diving technology; artifact analysis; heritage management; iconography; relevance to modern maritime research. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ships and Shipwrecks of the Americas. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how ships and seafaring shaped the history and culture of the Western Hemisphere from 1492 through the American Civil War. Draws on archaeological discoveries and historical records to examine exploration, colonization, trade, naval conflict and technological innovation through the lens of maritime material culture. Reviews case studies of shipwrecks and other maritime sites, revealing the vessels, technologies and practices that connected cultures, facilitated economic systems and transformed warfare. From Indigenous watercraft to colonial gunboats, steamboats and Civil War submarines, engages with the archaeological evidence that illuminates change and continuity in the maritime world of the Americas. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in nautical archaeology of the Americas. TOPICS AND THEMES. Ship construction; ship rigging; seafaring technologies; European and American shipwreck archaeological case studies; Iberian voyages of exploration; Basque whaling; Spain’s maritime empire; Northern European maritime exploration; colonization; technological developments; economics and history of the Western Hemisphere; European-Indigenous relationships; Indigenous watercraft; Anglo-French wars; piracy and privateering; Revolutionary War; War of 1812; Shipping in the Commercial Age; canal transport; horse-powered boats; steamboats; packet ships; clipper ships; whaling fleets; Arctic exploration; Civil War naval warfare. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: European Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of human prehistory and history on the European continent and surrounding islands through the remains of material culture such as artifacts, human and animal remains, structures, landscapes and environments. Investigates the wide time span from the earliest Paleolithic hunter-gatherer hominids (up to two million years ago), through the Neolithic agricultural “revolution”, the metal ages, the classical civilizations of Greece and Rome, the medieval period and up to the modern era. Develops critical analysis skills using different types of information including archaeological site reports, academic papers, historical records and other primary sources to understand individual sites. Compares sites across space and time to form ideas of changing lifeways, technologies, and social and individual identities of past Europeans. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include human origins and migration; adaption and environment; domestication and agriculture; technological innovation and development; trade; social complexity, urbanization and state formation including hunter-gatherers, small scale societies, cities and empires; conflict and warfare; religion and ritual; art, music and culture; social, cultural and individual identity. Methodologies discussed include archaeological excavations, surveys, GIS, spatial analysis, analysis of landscapes and buildings, dating methods, artifact analysis, examination of human and animal remains, environmental and geoarchaeology, lab methods including ancient DNA, proteins, lipids, and stable isotopes, ethnographies and experimental archaeology. Class discussions may be thought-provoking and introduce new perspectives and material that students may not have encountered before. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Archaeology of Ancient Greece. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Greece from the Stone Age through the Hellenistic Period, concluding with the rise of Rome. Explores the material culture, art, architecture and social history of the Greek world across its major cultural phases, from the Bronze Age civilizations of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece to the flourishing of Classical Athens and the cosmopolitan Hellenistic kingdoms. Emphasizes the integration of archaeological evidence, ancient texts and artistic traditions to illuminate Greek religion, civic life, domestic space and cultural interactions across the Mediterranean. By examining key sites, monuments, artifacts and artistic achievements, students gain a comprehensive understanding of Greek society and its enduring legacy in Western civilization. TOPICS AND THEMES. Stone Age and Neolithic Greece; Bronze Age civilizations; Minoan Crete; Mycenaean palaces and the Trojan War; the Greek Dark Ages; Geometric period art and society; Archaic architecture, sculpture and vase painting; Classical Athens and the Acropolis; sanctuaries such as Delphi; fourth-century Greece and the rise of Macedon; Hellenistic art, architecture and urbanism; Greek houses and domestic mosaics; shipwreck archaeology; coinage and economic history; Greek religion and votive practices; interactions with Magna Graecia and the wider Mediterranean; Greek artistic and cultural legacy in Rome and later neoclassicism. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with CLAS 353.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ancient Civilizations of the World. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores archaeological studies that have contributed to our understanding of the emergence and decline of states and civilizations between 3500 BCE and 1500 CE. Examines the complex origins of anthropology and archaeology within the discourses on "civilization" and comparative models of human development. Explores the political organization, social structures, cultural practices and technological advancements of complex societies in regions such as the Near East, Africa, Europe, India, China, Mesoamerica and North America. Explores theoretical frameworks, methodological approaches and the interpretation of archaeological and related data to comprehend the nature of these complex societies in various parts of the world. TOPICS AND THEMES. Theories of civilization and socio-political organization of ancient societies, neo-evolutionary models of social complexity, agricultural societies and the rise of states, archaeological evidence of hierarchy, heterarchy, urbanism, and state formation in ancient societies, environmental factors in the rise and fall of complex societies; trade, warfare and cooperation in ancient societies; comparative studies of complex societies, states and empires in various regions of the world; the collapse of ancient states and lessons for modern states. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Archaeological Artifact Conservation. (3-3). Credit 4. COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides an in-depth introduction to the theory and practice of conserving archaeological artifacts, emphasizing the stabilization and long-term preservation of materials recovered from terrestrial and underwater sites. Examines both theoretical grounding and extensive hands-on experience in the laboratory, learning to assess artifact condition, select appropriate treatment strategies and apply conservation techniques to a wide range of materials including organics, ceramics, glass and metals. Through lectures, readings and laboratory exercises, students explore the chemical and physical principles underlying conservation, the ethical considerations surrounding intervention and preservation and the role of conservation within archaeological research and curation. TOPICS AND THEMES. Principles of archaeological conservation and preservation; conservation ethics and documentation; health and safety in the conservation laboratory; adhesives and consolidants; conservation of organic materials including bone, ivory, wood, leather, textiles and rope; stabilization of siliceous materials such as ceramics, glass and stone; corrosion processes and treatment of archaeological metals including iron, copper alloys, lead, tin and precious metals; electrolytic and chemical cleaning methods; desalinization and drying processes; material identification and condition assessment; factors of decay in burial environments; field conservation practices; reconstruction techniques and aesthetic reintegration; and integration of conservation data into archaeological interpretation and collections management. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Science, Pseudoscience and Critical Thinking in Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examination of extraordinary claims made across a wide spectrum of media in the fields of anthropology, biological anthropology and archaeology. Emphasis on distinguishing science from pseudoscience through application of the scientific method, logical reasoning and critical evaluation of empirical evidence. Writing-intensive assignments develop students’ critical thinking, analytical skills and ability to communicate effectively about complex and sometimes controversial issues in anthropology and in broader scientific inquiry. Attention to recognizing and refuting poor scientific reasoning, evaluation of media portrayal of science and clear dissemination of ideas within and beyond academic contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of science, pseudoscience, pathological science, junk science and anti-science; scientific hoaxes, frauds and exaggeration of evidence; the scientific method and the use and misuse of statistics and illustrations; distortions of anthropological and scientific knowledge across a variety of media platforms, including social media and ‘fake news’; history of the discipline of anthropology; IQ testing, race, and racism; creation science, natural selection, and evolution; cryptozoology, bigfoot and aquatic apes; the use, misuse and abuse of the archaeological record in both scientific and popular discourse; the supernatural realm; and conspiracy theories, climate science and vaccine efficacy. Course discussions may also engage diverse and sometimes unfamiliar perspectives, reflecting a variety of contexts – scientific, professional, political, cultural – in which group communication occurs. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: ANTH 210 or ANTH 205.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Anthropological Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the history and foundations of anthropological theory, connecting these historical concepts to contemporary professional concerns. Critiques the core assumptions, preferred questions and specific methods associated with major theoretical schools. Engages diverse points of view to examine current social issues and applied problems, fostering respect for cultural and human biological diversity. Develops comprehensive expertise in articulating theoretical explanations for research questions, identifying the major theorist(s) credited for theory development and detailing how theory is currently used by anthropologists. Practices critical synthesis of theoretical knowledge within existing disciplinary frameworks. Evaluates arguments by questioning the type and sufficiency of evidence presented. Assesses the cultural position, background and historical context of authors conveying messages, including whether the argument is shaped by a particular historical moment or if the author has an agenda. Requires active application of theoretical models against individual student areas of interest. TOPICS AND THEMES. Explores foundational classics; analyzes epistemology, axiology and related conceptual frameworks; considers the Nature/Nurture Debate; investigation of functional thinking, processes, structures and pragmatics; transformation and evolution; symbols and coherence; cultural materialism and economies; and critical advocacy, feminisms, Post Modernism, post-structuralism and the ontological turn. Prerequisite: ANTH 210 or ANTH 205.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Archaeological Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. An advanced undergraduate course reviewing the history of scientific archaeological thought, major theoretical paradigms and current trends in archaeology, provides firm grounding in the development and current application of archaeological theory, a fundamental component of all students’ training in archaeology, no matter their specialty. Covers the major theoretical “movements” in the development of anthropological archaeology, as well as important intellectual developments in other disciplines which have influenced explanation in archaeology (e.g., cultural anthropology, geology, evolutionary biology and other social sciences). Historically oriented, reviews how archaeological theory has evolved in the past century and how contemporary archaeologists use theory to explain variability in the material-culture record of past humans. TOPICS AND THEMES. History of scientific archaeological exploration; major theoretical paradigms and movements in archaeological theory; current trends in archaeology; intellectual developments from other disciplines that influenced archaeological thought. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Anthropological Writing. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Practices critical reading and writing skills through the study and discussion of anthropologically relevant literature. Examines various styles and formats of anthropological writing, treating the discipline as an ongoing conversation and discourse community. Develops writing proficiency necessary for professional participation in anthropology and related career paths, including the interpretation, critique and evaluation of scientific papers. Emphasizes effective peer review and the capacity to accept constructive criticism. Cultivates clear communication strategies for discussing complex anthropological topics with both academic and broader audiences. Organizes written work using careful and critical thought. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers common citation styles, including the appropriate inclusion of primary sources. Analyzes the scientific publication process and Reference Management Software (RMS) usage. Studies professional writing, including personal statements, cover letters, CVs and resumes, prepared as part of an application packet for jobs, internships or graduate school. Explores writing clearly and concisely for diverse audiences, including rewriting scholarly work for non-academic audiences and developing an original research paper on a topic of the student’s choosing. Examines various styles of scientific papers, including research articles, review articles, programmatic essays, ethnographies and popular media. Practices peer review techniques and critical analysis of complex texts. Verbal communication and synthesis of anthropological research in small group settings and an individual oral presentation. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Naval Warfare and Warships in Ancient Greece and Rome. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys topics such as Greek and Roman warships, naval warfare, naval strategy and tactics, drawing upon archaeological evidence, literary documentation and iconographic material. Covers the development of Mediterranean naval power from the Bronze Age (including Ancient Egypt and the mythical Trojan War) to the Imperial Roman Navy. Examines Greek naval dominance during the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars, the evolution of warships such as triremes, Roman naval organization and imperial fleets, and the technological, strategic and political dimensions of naval warfare. Students analyze ship construction, rigging, armament and naval technology within their historical and cultural context. TOPICS AND THEMES. Bronze Age Mediterranean warships; Egyptian naval warfare; Bronze Age naval battles; Athenian Navy; trireme; Greco-Persian Wars (499-449 B.C.); Peloponnesian Wars (431-404 B.C.); naval campaigns of Alexander the Great; Age of Titans; Greek war machines and weapons; Greek naval monuments; Phoenician Navy; Punic Navy; Roman naval organization; Roman Imperial Navy; Roman warships and tactics; Mare Nostrum; Punic Wars (264-146 B.C.); Roman Navy in the Eastern Mediterranean; naval campaigns of Julius Caesar; naval campaigns of Octavian; Roman fluvial warships; Roman naval shipwrecks; Roman war machines and tactics; ship construction; rigging; armament; naval technology; maritime strategy; naval logistics; naval archaeology; iconography; material culture; maritime military history; technological arms race at sea. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with CLAS 417.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Pirates, Privateers and Sea Raiders. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Provides an in-depth survey of the history and archaeology of piracy, privateering and sea raiding from ancient times in the eastern Mediterranean through the Viking Era in the Northern Atlantic and the rise of piracy in the New World and Caribbean during the 16th–18th centuries. Examines archaeological evidence of pirate ventures, the social organization of pirate and privateering communities and the economic, political and cultural effects of piracy on empires, trade networks and maritime law. Explores the sensationalism of pirate legend in literature, film and music, and introduces contemporary piracy in Africa, the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia. Through lectures, readings, presentations and research assignments, students develop critical skills to evaluate primary and secondary sources, analyze cause-and-effect relationships and assess the broader impact of piracy across time and regions. TOPICS. May include: origins, causes and major periods of piracy, privateering and sea raiding; archaeological evidence of pirate activity in the Mediterranean, Northern Atlantic, Caribbean and Americas; Viking, European and New World piracy; raids, privateering and colonial interactions; social structure, codes of conduct and daily life of pirate communities; economic and political effects of piracy on trade, colonialism, slavery and national sovereignty; sensationalism of pirate legend in literature, film and music; cultural responses to piracy; female pirates and gender dynamics in seafaring communities; contemporary piracy in Africa, the Indian Ocean and Southeast Asia; case studies of shipwrecks, pirate lairs and maritime settlements; research methods and critical evaluation of primary and secondary sources. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Dental Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the methods used to study teeth, a subdiscipline central to biological anthropology (the study of human evolution and variation), bioarchaeology (the study of human remains in archaeological contexts), anatomy, dentistry and palaeontology (the study of fossil life). Explores the essential questions regarding dental analysis: How are teeth studied, and what insights can dental research provide? Gains in-depth experience with the core concepts of dental anatomy, dental development, dental ecology and dental evolution. Develops confidence in identifying teeth in both human and non-human primates and their closest living relatives. Analyzes current literature concerning dental form, function and evolutionary patterns. Cultivates critical thinking abilities necessary for evaluating cutting-edge dental research and effectively presenting and writing about these findings. TOPICS AND THEMES. Considers dental anatomy and introduces the tribosphenic molar as a key evolutionary feature. Analyzes the evolution of mammalian mastication and its implications for dietary adaptation. Explores evolutionary developmental biology as it relates to tooth formation and variation. Studies dental eruption patterns, life history traits and dentition patterns in primates. Investigates dental ecology and applies methods for reconstructing ancient diets. Examines dietary reconstruction techniques including macro- and microwear analysis, enamel thickness and dental topography. Reviews the dental-pulp complex, dental pathology and the role of dental form in understanding phylogenetic relationships among human and non-human primates. Prerequisites: ANTH 225 or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Medical Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces medical anthropology, the subfield exploring the biological and cultural dimensions of health, illness and healing across diverse societies. Defines and discusses key concepts, such as health, illness and disease, in relation to various social, environmental, political and evolutionary contexts. Analyzes the interconnections among micro- and macrobiological, cultural, social and political determinants to construct a holistic view of human health. Engages with contemporary and emerging issues in health and healthcare, emphasizing the comparative analysis of global medical systems. Compares and contrasts biomedicine with other ethnomedical systems to evaluate its role within diverse cultural contexts. Develops critical thinking, reading, writing and collaboration skills for engaging with multiple perspectives on health. Note that course content may include complex or sensitive topics designed to foster critical engagement. TOPICS AND THEMES. Surveys foundational theories and methodologies. Analyzes cultural beliefs and environmental influences on health, including ecological and evolutionary disease patterning. Explores health-related behaviors, mental health, medical systems and explanatory models across diverse cultural contexts. Examines environmental health challenges, globalization and infectious disease. Considers gender, race/racism, social inequality and health disparities. Discusses professional applications and emerging issues in the subdiscipline. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ancient Egypt I - The Rise of Egypt. (3-0). Credit 3. Archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from earliest times to the end of the New Kingdom period. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with RELS 436.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Completion of ANTH 436 or RELS 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ancient Egypt II - Egypt in Decline. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from the end of the New Kingdom through the Graeco-Roman period, focusing on the years 1185–30 BCE. Examines the decline of pharaonic power, the rise of foreign influences and the resilience of Egyptian society under Libyan, Nubian, Persian and Ptolemaic rule. Reviews the interplay between political, social and cultural dynamics, exploring Egyptian adaptations to Hellenistic dominance, while tracing continuity and change in art, religion, literature and urban development. Through lectures, readings and analyses of primary and secondary sources, students gain a humanistic understanding of Egyptian civilization during its final dynastic phases and develop skills in interpreting archaeological, textual and iconographic evidence. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues pertaining to ancient Egypt. TOPICS AND THEMES. Decline of pharaonic authority; fragmentation of the Egyptian state; Libyan, Nubian and Persian interventions; internal political strife and social change; resilience of Egyptian cultural identity; Ptolemaic dynasty and Hellenistic influence; Cleopatra VII and the last Ptolemies; Alexandria as a cultural and economic center; Greco-Egyptian art, religion and literature; continuity and transformation of Egyptian traditions; interactions between foreign rulers and Egyptian elites; archaeological and textual methods for reconstructing late Egyptian history; humanistic approaches to interpreting material culture; synthesis of historical, artistic and archaeological evidence. Prerequisites: Completion of ANTH 436 or RELS 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with RELS 438.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Quantitative Ethnographic Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces quantitative ethnographic field methods commonly used in anthropological research to formally test hypotheses. Explores the benefits and challenges of applying structured, quantitative techniques to the study of complex cultural phenomena within a field largely dominated by qualitative methods. Covers best practices for managing and analyzing anthropological datasets. Surveys common ethnographic methods designed to enhance comparability and analytical rigor of ethnographic research, including structured interviews, text analysis and network analysis. Through hands-on assignments, provides practical experience in developing and executing small-scale research projects. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics include ethical considerations in field research, research design, data management, statistical analysis, structured interviews, online survey tools, standardized observation, network analysis, text analysis and cultural consensus analysis. Also includes student participation in all stages of the research process, including research design, data collection, data management and analysis, and write-up. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Cultural Heritage and Resource Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Evaluation of modern ideas about how and why archaeological, architectural, ethnographic, and natural resources should be preserved and presented to current and future societies; critical examination of the theories, methods, regulations, and ethics that guide efforts to preserve and protect cultural heritage within a context of past endeavors and future directions. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: The Archaeology and Anthropology of Foraging Societies. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the archaeology and anthropology of foraging (hunting and gathering) societies in time and space. Includes an overview of archaeology focused on foraging societies and current methodological and theoretical issues, especially the use of ethnographic and environmental data. Investigates ecologically oriented case studies of late Pleistocene and Holocene hunter-gatherers paired with the ethnographic record used to interpret these sites. Archaeological case studies will have an emphasis on land-use, site-structure and site formation analyses. Ethnographic case studies will focus on the diversity of hunting and gathering societies, change in these societies through time and discussion of forager economies, with specific attention to critiquing ethnohistoric accounts and the applicability of these case studies to the archaeological record. TOPICS AND THEMES. Forager (hunter-gatherer) variation in different environments; forager variation through time; forager social structures; forager mobility; forager subsistence; socio-political complexity in foraging societies; ethnographic critiques; archaeology of foraging societies; resource management; foragers in the modern world and change in forager societies in the recent past; archaeological site structure; lithic analysis; site formation processes; archaeological site survey; archaeological theory of foragers; site modeling and resource modeling. This course may incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues relevant to anthropology. Course content may include complex or sensitive topics and is designed to foster respectful, evidence-based discussion and critical engagement with multiple perspectives, skills essential for navigating a diverse and changing world. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Quantitative Ethnographic Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. Quantitative data collection and analytical methods employed by anthropologists including standardized observation, structured interviews, demography and network analysis; emphasizes hands-on assignments involving data collection among local community. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

subject: ANTH

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Analytical Methods in Archaeology and Conservation. (3-0). Credit 3. Conventional and advanced techniques used for artifact material analysis and artifact documentation; material analysis is the way that we study artifacts, both in structure and elemental composition; includes photography and artifact sketching, computer modeling, laser digitization, computer image photogrammetry, 3D printing and XRF elemental analysis. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in anthropology or approval of instructor.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Cultural Heritage and Resource Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Evaluation of modern ideas about how and why archaeological, architectural, ethnographic, and natural resources should be preserved and presented to current and future societies; critical examination of the theories, methods, regulations, and ethics that guide efforts to preserve and protect cultural heritage within a context of past endeavors and future directions. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

subject: ANTH
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Medical Anthropology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces medical anthropology, the subfield exploring the biological and cultural dimensions of health, illness and healing across diverse societies. Defines and discusses key concepts, such as health, illness and disease, in relation to various social, environmental, political and evolutionary contexts. Analyzes the interconnections among micro- and macrobiological, cultural, social and political determinants to construct a holistic view of human health. Engages with contemporary and emerging issues in health and healthcare, emphasizing the comparative analysis of global medical systems. Compares and contrasts biomedicine with other ethnomedical systems to evaluate its role within diverse cultural contexts. Develops critical thinking, reading, writing and collaboration skills for engaging with multiple perspectives on health. Note that course content may include complex or sensitive topics designed to foster critical engagement. TOPICS AND THEMES. Surveys foundational theories and methodologies. Analyzes cultural beliefs and environmental influences on health, including ecological and evolutionary disease patterning. Explores health-related behaviors, mental health, medical systems and explanatory models across diverse cultural contexts. Examines environmental health challenges, globalization and infectious disease. Considers gender, race/racism, social inequality and health disparities. Discusses professional applications and emerging issues in the subdiscipline. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

subject: AREN
prerequisite_text: Sophomore classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Architectural Engineering Foundations. (2-0). Credit 2. Introduction to the broad field and professional practice of architectural engineering, architectural engineering systems, and the role of the architectural engineer; emphasis on professional engineering design services, design and construction processes and documents, building envelope and materials, structural systems, mechanical systems, lighting systems, building systems integration, building codes and standards, fire safety, professional attributes of architectural engineers, and issues of human performance requirements and sustainability at relates to building system design. Prerequisite: Sophomore classification or approval of instructor.

subject: AREN
course_title: FUND BUILD INFO MODL ARCH ENGR
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Fundamentals of Building Information Modeling for Architectural Engineering. (2-3). Credit 3. Application of the fundamentals of engineering design, document production, and interdisciplinary coordination utilizing design and drafting software; application of software to model shapes, structures, and systems in 3D with parametric accuracy, precision, and ease; topics include streamline documentation work, with instant revisions to plans, elevations, schedules, and sections as projects change; and introduction of specialty toolsets; production of structural and mechanical-electrical-plumbing systems in a 3-D model.

subject: AREN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253, or equivalent, or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in PHYS 206; grade of C or better in ENGR 216 or PHYS 216.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Engineering Mechanics - Statics and Dynamics for Architectural Engineers. (4-0). Credit 4. Principles of statics, kinematics, and kinetics, with particular attention to architectural engineering applications; general principles of mechanics; concurrent force systems; statics of particles; equivalent force/moment systems; centroids and center of gravity; equilibrium of rigid bodies; trusses, and frames; internal forces in structural members; friction; second moments of areas; force action related to displacement, velocity, and acceleration of rigid bodies; kinematics of plane motion; kinetics of translation and rotation; mass moment of inertia; vibration; work, energy, and power; impulse and momentum. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253, or equivalent, or concurrent enrollment; grade of C or better in PHYS 206; grade of C or better in ENGR 216 or PHYS 216.

subject: AREN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AREN 200 and AREN 221; grade of C or better in AREN 281 or concurrent enrollment.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Architectural Engineering Systems. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the architectural engineering discipline equipping with comprehensive knowledge of various building systems covering the analysis, integration and application of the engineering design process to solve problems associated with the design and operation of building systems; communication of solutions to technical problems of building system, through writing, presentations and team interactions, typical for architectural engineers in the building industry; emphasis on the engineering design process in architectural engineering structural systems for integrity and resilience, mechanical systems for heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning, electrical lighting, power generation and energy; fire safety, architectural acoustics and introduces students to building codes and standards to be able to interface, integrate and optimize to resolve coordination issues among different building systems; and sustainability aspects of building systems including net zero energy, water, waste and carbon. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AREN 200 and AREN 221; grade of C or better in AREN 281 or concurrent enrollment.

subject: AREN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AREN 221, MEEN 221, MEEN 225, or CVEN 221; grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Thermal-Fluid Sciences I for Architectural Engineers. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamental theory and practical application of thermal-fluid sciences adapted for architectural engineering; conservation laws, energy conversion, thermodynamic properties, open and closed systems analysis, psychrometric analysis, vapor and gas cycles with emphasis on refrigeration cycles; fluid behavior laws; dimensional analysis for external and internal flows. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AREN 221, MEEN 221, MEEN 225, or CVEN 221; grade of C or better in MATH 251 or MATH 253.

subject: AREN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AREN 310 or equivalent.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Thermal-Fluid Sciences II for Architectural Engineers. (3-0). Credit 3. Continued theory and application of thermal-fluid sciences adapted for architectural engineering; open channel flow, pumps, conduction, convection, and radiation heat transfer; heat exchangers; introduction to computational fluid dynamics and computational heat transfer for building applications. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AREN 310 or equivalent.

subject: AREN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in AREN 300 and AREN 310; or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Mechanical Systems for Buildings. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to qualitative and quantitative engineering concepts of mechanical systems for buildings for architectural engineers, including HVAC systems, control of indoor air pollutants and fire suppression systems; emphasis on thermal behavior of buildings and building envelopes, human comfort requirements and psychometrics, thermal load calculations, HVAC systems/equipment, design of space air-conditioning and its relationship to architectural design, mechanical systems for indoor air quality and for fire suppression. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AREN 300 and AREN 310; or approval of instructor.

subject: AREN

subject: AREN

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Architectural Engineering Design I. (3-3). Credit 4. Instruction and practice in the design process applied to an architectural engineering design project; application of establishing customer need, determining requirements in terms of function and performance, developing alternative design concepts, performing trade-off studies among performance, cost and schedule, embodiment and detail design and the iteration of the above steps; major architectural engineering design project. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in AREN 330, AREN 311, and CVEN 345.

subject: ARSC
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Contemporary Issues in Science - The Environment. (3-0). Credit 3. This team-taught, interdisciplinary course is designed to build scientific literacy by examining contemporary issues in science - current questions, discoveries and challenges that shape our understanding of the environment. Topics may include climate change, energy systems, plastics and pollution, agriculture, water and food safety, biodiversity, environmental health and chemicals and drugs (including vaccines). Students will learn to evaluate scientific claims and critically analyze how science is presented in the news, on television and on social media. Cross-listed with CHEM 105.

subject: ARSC
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Perspectives on Secondary Teaching. (1-1). Credit 1. Study of adolescents in a variety of school and community settings; overview of issues in secondary education and discussions around qualities of effective teaching. Exploration of issues related to professionalism, state standards, classroom management and effective instruction. This experience is designed to help students evaluate their interest in a secondary education career and serves as the recommended introductory course for aggieTEACH-Arts & Sciences. It assists in assessing a student's aptitude, foundational knowledge and initial skills for pursuing secondary teaching certification.

subject: ASTR
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in ASTR 314 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Astrophysical Research Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. Background and tools used in modern astrophysical research, including reduction of photometric and spectroscopic data, signal-to-noise and error calculations and order-of-magnitude estimates. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in ASTR 314 or approval of instructor.

subject: ASTR
prerequisite_text: ASTR 314.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Stars and Extrasolar Planets. (3-0). Credit 3. How stars are born, how internal structure changes, nuclear fuel burned and ultimate fate; extrasolar planet detection, formation, properties and habitability. Prerequisite: ASTR 314.

subject: ASTR
prerequisite_text: ASTR 314.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Extragalactic Astronomy and Cosmology. (3-0). Credit 3. Physical makeup of individual galaxies and large scale structure in the universe; origin and eventual fate of the universe; interpretation of observational data as it relates to baryonic matter, Dark Matter and cosmological models with Dark Energy. Prerequisite: ASTR 314.

subject: ASTR

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Advanced Astrophysical Research Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ASTR 320 or approval of instructor.
