prerequisite_text: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Written Communication in Biochemical Research. (2-0). Credit 2. Examination of research literature to define a scientific problem, critical barrier to progress, or hypothesis of significance; development of experimental and/or theoretical projects (Specific Aims) designed to address or test the scientific problem, barrier to progress, or hypothesis; learning grantsmanship by analyzing and critiquing National Institutes of Health grant proposals; formulation, presentation, evaluation, and defending of Specific Aims. Prerequisites: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.

subject: BICH
prerequisite_text: BICH 603 and BICH 631; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Oral Communication in Biochemical Research. (1-0). Credit 1. Oral communication techniques necessary to convey biochemical information effectively and to prepare for the oral presentation as part of the preliminary exam; biochemistry specific techniques that relate to the scientific method, significance and biochemical literature, the presentation of specific aims, and the description of experimental strategies or results. Prerequisites: BICH 603 and BICH 631; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.

subject: BICH
prerequisite_text: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Biomolecular Nuclear Magnetic Resonance Spectroscopy Theory and Practice. (1-0). Credit 1. Theoretical and practical applications of biomolecular NMR spectroscopy. Prerequisites: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.

subject: BICH
prerequisite_text: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Cellular Biophysics. (1-0). Credit 1. Exploration of a range of current topics in physical biology and systems biology including diffusion and network motifs. Prerequisites: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.

subject: BICH
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification in biochemistry, biochemistry and molecular biophysics, genetics, genetics and genomics, or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Mechanisms of Cell Division. (1-0). Credit 1. Mitotic cell cycle; progression of biochemical and morphological phases and events; duplication of cellular constituents and segregation into daughter cells. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in biochemistry, biochemistry and molecular biophysics, genetics, genetics and genomics, or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with GENE 616.

subject: BICH
prerequisite_text: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Optical Spectroscopy. (1-0). Credit 1. Overview of major optical spectroscopy techniques, including absorption, fluorescence, infrared and Raman spectroscopy; special emphasis on fundamental physical principles of these techniques and their applications in biology. Prerequisites: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.

subject: BICH
prerequisite_text: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Cryo-Electron Microscopy of Molecular Machines. (1-0). Credit 1. Exploration of current topics in structural biology; focus on cryo-electron microscopy; visualization techniques for three-dimensional structures of macromolecules; use of electron microscopes and computational tools; review of basic visualization steps; discussion of primary literature. Prerequisites: BICH 603 or approval of instructor; graduate classification in biochemistry or biochemistry and molecular biophysics.

prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.

subject: BIMS
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in CHEM 228 or CHEM 258; PHYS 207 or grade of C or better in PHYS 202; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Biomedical Genetics. (3-0). Credit 3. Study of modern genetics with an emphasis on biomedical and health-related applications of the mammalian genome. Topics include classical Mendelian inheritance, pedigree and genetic risk analysis, population genetics, quantitative genetics and the molecular basis of gene structure and function, including DNA replication, transcription, mutation and gene regulation. The course examines how genetic variation and chromosomal abnormalities contribute to disease and phenotypic diversity, and introduces advanced concepts in cytogenetics, epigenetics, cancer genetics and genomics. Contemporary applications such as genome sequencing, gene therapy, personalized medicine and associated ethical considerations are also addressed. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: GENE 301, GENE 302, GENE 315, GENE-320 or BIMS-320. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 228 or CHEM 258; PHYS 207 or grade of C or better in PHYS 202; junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with GENE 320.

subject: BIOL
prerequisite_text: BIOL 112 and CHEM 120.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Molecular Cell Biology. (3-0). Credit 3. This course covers how cells are built, powered and regulated. Topics include macromolecules; membranes and transport; energy production and conversion; genome organization and evolution; DNA structure and replication; gene expression and regulation; intracellular trafficking; cytoskeleton; cell communication and electrical signaling; cell division and cancer. Additional topics may be presented based on time and instructor expertise. The course emphasizes evidence-based reasoning, quantitative skills and core experimental methods. Prerequisites: BIOL 112 and CHEM 120.

subject: BIOL
prerequisite_text: GENE 302; BIOL 351.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Bacterial Genetics. (3-0). Credit 3. A problem oriented course surveying the manipulation and mechanisms of genetic systems in bacteria; recombination, gene structure and regulation of bacterial genes, plasmids and phages. Prerequisites: GENE 302; BIOL 351. Cross-listed with GENE 406.

subject: BIOL
prerequisite_text: BICH 431, BIOL 213 or GENE 431.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Biological Clocks. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of the basic mechanisms of biological timing; in depth study of clocks in model organisms and the relationship between clocks and human health and disease. Prerequisites: BICH 431, BIOL 213 or GENE 431.

subject: BIOL
prerequisite_text: BIOL 351 or BICH 431.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Synthetic Biology of Microbes. (3-0). Credit 3. Underlying technical basis for synthetic biology; tools used to generate recombinant molecules; genetic circuitry and modules applied to bacteria; design and fabrication of genes, biological components and entire organisms; survey actual and theoretical applications. Prerequisites: BIOL 351 or BICH 431.

subject: BIOL
prerequisite_text: BIOL 213, GENE 302, or GENE 303; BICH 410 or BICH 440.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Cell Biology. (3-0). Credit 3. Structure, function, and biogenesis of cells and their components; interpretation of dynamic processes of cells, including protein trafficking, motility, signaling and proliferation. Prerequisites: BIOL 213, GENE 302, or GENE 303; BICH 410 or BICH 440.

subject: BIOL
prerequisite_text: BIOL 213 or GENE 302; BICH 410 or BICH 440.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Developmental Biology. (3-0). Credit 3. Concepts of development in systems ranging from bacteriophage to the mammalian embryo; use of recombinant DNA technology and embryo engineering to unravel the relationships between growth and differentiation, morphogenesis and commitment, aging and cancer. Prerequisite: BIOL 213 or GENE 302; BICH 410 or BICH 440.

subject: BIOL
prerequisite_text: GENE 302 or equivalent, or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Plant Molecular Biology. (3-0). Credit 3. This course will explore the molecular aspects of plant growth, development, reproduction and evolution, with an emphasis on gene manipulation and the practical applications of plant molecular biology. Prerequisites: GENE 302 or equivalent, or approval of instructor.

subject: BIOL
prerequisite_text: BIOL 213 and PSYC 235, or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Cellular Neuroscience. (3-0). Credit 3. Cell biology, molecular biology and biophysics of neurons as it pertains to their fundamental role in the physiological basis of behavior; study of how neurons create, maintain and exploit electrical signals for information coding and transmission; principles of electrical and chemical signaling between neurons, and the role of intracellular signaling for signal modulation and synaptic plasticity; exploration of a broad range of state-of-the-art molecular tools currently used to study the nervous system, and the cellular basis for many of the most common neurological disorders affecting humans as well as the strategies and therapies for their treatment. Prerequisites: BIOL 213 and PSYC 235, or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with NRSC 428

subject: BIOL

Prerequisite: Junior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: BIOL
prerequisite_text: BIOL 111, BIOL 112 and BIOL 213; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Biology Through Film. (3-0). Credit 3. This course offers an innovative exploration of fundamental concepts in biology through their portrayal in film, highlighting the intersection of scientific discovery, medicine and society. Students will engage with primary scientific literature to develop a firsthand understanding of the discovery process underlying topics such as neurodegenerative disease, genetic engineering, addiction and disease transmission. Class discussions will connect these foundational insights to critical analyses of how such themes are represented in film, encouraging students to evaluate both the processes of scientific discovery and their societal implications. Through this dual approach, the course fosters scientific literacy, ethical reasoning and a deeper appreciation for the relationship between science and society. Prerequisites: BIOL 111, BIOL 112 and BIOL 213; junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: FDA Good Laboratory and Clinical Practices. (3-0). Credit 3. Implementation of Good Laboratory Practices (GLP) for the submission of preclinical studies and use of Good Clinical Practices (GCP) in clinical trials in accordance with Food and Drug Administration (FDA) regulations; includes similarities and differences in GLP and GCP critical for the introduction of new drugs and medical devices. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: BMEN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Bioelectromagnetism. (3-0). Credit 3. Electric, magnetic and electromagnetic phenomena in association with biological tissues; source modeling based on physiological current including line and volume conductor models as well as electromagnetic-based stimulation, sensing and imaging. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: BMEN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Biophotonics. (3-0). Credit 3. Theory and application of optical instrumentation, including light sources, lasers, detectors, and optical fibers; instrumentation and engineering in biomedical applications of optics in therapeutics, diagnostics, and biosensing. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: BMEN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Molecular and Cellular Biomechanics. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduces biomolecules and their assemblies that play structural and dynamical roles in subcellular to cellular level mechanics, with emphasis on quantitative/theoretical descriptions, and discussions of the relevant experiment approaches to probe these nano to micro-scale phenomena; including topics in (1) self-assembly of cytoskeleton and biomembranes, (2) molecular motors, (3) cell motility, and mechanotransduction. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: BMEN
prerequisite_text: Approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Biomaterials Compatibility. (3-0). Credit 3. Relevance of mechanical and physical properties to implant selection and design; effect of the body environment on metallic, ceramic and plastic materials; tissue engineering; rejection mechanisms used by the body to maintain homeostasis regulatory requirements. Prerequisites: Approval of instructor.

prerequisite_text: CHEM 601.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Analytical Chemistry II. (3-0). Credit 3. Modern analytical techniques, spectroscopies, chromatography, and "hyphenated" methods such as GC-FTIR, GC-MS, HPLC-MS, CE-LIF, and CE-MS are examined from the perspective of surface analysis, fundamentals of separation science and structural characterization of complex molecular systems. Prerequisite: CHEM 601.

subject: CHEM
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Advanced Polymer Chemistry. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamentals of polymer chemistry; mechanistic principles and methods of modern polymer synthesis; correlation of chemistry, structure, and properties of advanced polymeric materials; includes topics on contemporary polymer chemistry, polymer physics, and characterization techniques. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: CHEM
prerequisite_text: CHEM 648 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Analytical Spectroscopy. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamentals of optical spectroscopy and applications; quantum mechanical description of light-matter interaction, linear and nonlinear spectroscopy, optics and spectroscopic instrumentation, optical signal detection and data acquisition/ processing, applications of spectroscopic techniques in nanoscience. Prerequisite: CHEM 648 or approval of instructor.

subject: CHEM
prerequisite_text: CHEM 328 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Chemical Kinetics. (3-0). Credit 3. Present theories about chemical reaction rates and mechanisms. Prerequisite: CHEM 328 or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_text: Graduate classification in engineering.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Multicriteria Assessment of Sustainable Processes. (3-0). Credit 3. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in engineering.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Risk Engineering. (3-0). Credit 3. subject: CHEN

Prerequisites: Graduate classification in engineering.

prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Archaeology of Ancient Greece. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology of ancient Greece from the Stone Age through the Hellenistic Period, concluding with the rise of Rome. Explores the material culture, art, architecture and social history of the Greek world across its major cultural phases, from the Bronze Age civilizations of Minoan Crete and Mycenaean Greece to the flourishing of Classical Athens and the cosmopolitan Hellenistic kingdoms. Emphasizes the integration of archaeological evidence, ancient texts and artistic traditions to illuminate Greek religion, civic life, domestic space and cultural interactions across the Mediterranean. By examining key sites, monuments, artifacts and artistic achievements, students gain a comprehensive understanding of Greek society and its enduring legacy in Western civilization. TOPICS AND THEMES. Stone Age and Neolithic Greece; Bronze Age civilizations; Minoan Crete; Mycenaean palaces and the Trojan War; the Greek Dark Ages; Geometric period art and society; Archaic architecture, sculpture and vase painting; Classical Athens and the Acropolis; sanctuaries such as Delphi; fourth-century Greece and the rise of Macedon; Hellenistic art, architecture and urbanism; Greek houses and domestic mosaics; shipwreck archaeology; coinage and economic history; Greek religion and votive practices; interactions with Magna Graecia and the wider Mediterranean; Greek artistic and cultural legacy in Rome and later neoclassicism. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ANTH 353.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Naval Warfare and Warships in Ancient Greece and Rome. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys topics such as Greek and Roman warships, naval warfare, naval strategy and tactics, drawing upon archaeological evidence, literary documentation and iconographic material. Covers the development of Mediterranean naval power from the Bronze Age (including Ancient Egypt and the mythical Trojan War) to the Imperial Roman Navy. Examines Greek naval dominance during the Persian and Peloponnesian Wars, the evolution of warships such as triremes, Roman naval organization and imperial fleets, and the technological, strategic and political dimensions of naval warfare. Students analyze ship construction, rigging, armament and naval technology within their historical and cultural context. TOPICS AND THEMES. Bronze Age Mediterranean warships; Egyptian naval warfare; Bronze Age naval battles; Athenian Navy; trireme; Greco-Persian Wars (499-449 B.C.); Peloponnesian Wars (431-404 B.C.); naval campaigns of Alexander the Great; Age of Titans; Greek war machines and weapons; Greek naval monuments; Phoenician Navy; Punic Navy; Roman naval organization; Roman Imperial Navy; Roman warships and tactics; Mare Nostrum; Punic Wars (264-146 B.C.); Roman Navy in the Eastern Mediterranean; naval campaigns of Julius Caesar; naval campaigns of Octavian; Roman fluvial warships; Roman naval shipwrecks; Roman war machines and tactics; ship construction; rigging; armament; naval technology; maritime strategy; naval logistics; naval archaeology; iconography; material culture; maritime military history; technological arms race at sea. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, ANTH 202 or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ANTH 417.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (SPCH 1315) Public Speaking. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles, practice and criticism of public speaking. Emphasizes public speaking as more than performance, examining key skills, including audience analysis, research, organization, use of supporting materials and delivery techniques. Attention to ethical communication and sensitivity to diverse audiences across professional, political, religious, cultural and ideological contexts. Includes practice in informative, persuasive and group speaking, developing verbal and nonverbal communication strategies. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with skills essential for professional, academic and civic life. Builds competence in organizing ideas, supporting arguments, adapting them to varied audiences. Develops confidence in extemporaneous speaking, critical listening and communication across diverse contexts. Prepares students for leadership roles, workplace communication and active participation in public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about public speaking, such as viewing it only as performance or memorization, differ from research-based and practical perspectives. Develops understanding of speaking as a process involving invention, organization, style, delivery and audience adaptation, enhancing skills in extemporaneous speaking. Emphasizes that effective speaking requires ethical choices, critical thinking and sensitivity to diverse audiences as much as confidence in delivery. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of why public speaking matters in contemporary society; study of ethical principles in communication; development of confidence and listening skills; analysis of audiences and rhetorical situations; research and organization of supporting materials; crafting of effective introductions, bodies and conclusions; use of language and presentation aids; practice in informative, persuasive and ceremonial speaking; application of digital rhetoric and multimedia tools. Course speeches and examples may address diverse and sometimes controversial topics, reflecting perspectives represented in public life as well as subjects chosen by students; breadth of content emerges from student interests and experiences, and guidance from the instructor; also taught at Galveston campus.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (SPCH 2333) Group Communication and Discussion. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles, practice and research on small group communication. Focuses on definition, structure and functions of groups, including roles, norms, power and/or communication climate. Examines processes such as problem-solving, role-playing, decision-making, leadership, organization and/or conflict management. Attention to verbal and nonverbal codes, listening, relationships and/or cooperation as foundations for interaction and group productivity. Considers professional, political, religious, community and/or cultural contexts in which group communication occurs. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops both understanding and practical ability for effective participation and leadership in group settings with diverse participants across professional, academic and/or civic contexts. Builds competence in problem solving, decision-making and conflict management within teams. Strengthens ability to manage power dynamics, foster positive communication climates and/or adapt to cultural differences in group interaction. Enhances capacity for collaboration, organizational effectiveness and leadership in contexts where teamwork and collective decision-making are essential. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about group work differ from research-based perspectives. Develops understanding of the ways roles, norms, leadership and/or power can shape group interaction. Emphasizes that effective group communication requires cooperation, critical thinking and constructive conflict management to improve decision-making and outcomes. Explores how divergent or unfamiliar perspectives and backgrounds shape group interaction, offering insight into effective collaboration in diverse teams. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of group definition, structure and functions; study of roles, norms and power in group dynamics; analysis of communication climate and culture; approaches to problem solving and decision-making; strategies for leadership, organization and conflict management; examination of verbal and nonverbal codes and listening skills; techniques for fostering cooperation and productivity in groups. Course discussions may also engage with diverse and sometimes unfamiliar perspectives, reflecting the variety of professional, political, religious, community and/or cultural contexts in which group communication occurs.

Interview practice may include topics connected to identity, culture, ethics, work and/or participants’ personal lives. subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Enrollment in communication or telecommunication media studies majors, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication Technology Skills. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines principles and practices of communication technology in the digital domain. Surveys the history and standards of television, radio, video gaming, streaming media, e-publishing and/or social networking industries and markets. Focuses on production skills such as composing, recording and editing digital content, as well as media literacy across platforms, including the ability to evaluate social, cultural and/or ethical implications of communication technologies. Emphasizes media-centric strategic foresight to postulate regarding the future of the communication and technological landscape. Class applications may also draw on popular culture and/or current events, connecting course concepts to contemporary media environments. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds technical competence and media literacy skills applicable across professional, academic and civic contexts. Develops the skills necessary to create digital media content, adapt communication strategies to emerging technologies, tell stories across multiple media platforms and evaluate the impact of communication technologies on audiences and industries. Strengthens preparation for careers in journalism, media production, marketing, communication design, public relations and related fields where technological fluency and critical analysis are essential. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Builds understanding of how communication technologies shape interaction, identity and/or culture beyond their technical functions. Highlights how tools such as streaming platforms, social media and/or virtual environments influence professional practice, everyday communication and public dialogue. Clarifies both opportunities and challenges presented by digital media, including questions of access, ethics and/or social impact. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of the development and application of communication technologies across industries; exploration of audio, video, web and interactive media tools; analysis of digital platforms and markets; consideration of issues such as media convergence, intellectual property, ethics and sociocultural impact. Course work may incorporate case studies from popular culture and/or current events to connect course concepts with real-world practices. The course may include discourses and perspectives that are unfamiliar or controversial, reflecting the diversity of discourses relating to digital technologies and practices. Prerequisites: Enrollment in communication or telecommunication media studies majors, USLA-BA-JNS concentration or JOUR minor. Cross-listed with JOUR 230.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (SPCH 2335) Argumentation and Debate. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores principles of argumentation and skills of debate, with emphasis on reasoning, evidence, refutation and briefing. Examines how arguments are constructed, supported, challenged, revised and delivered. Considers the standards of sound reasoning, common fallacies and tests of evidence and credibility. Attention to ethical and cultural considerations in arguments, including analysis of audiences and contexts. Explores the role of debate in decision-making. Includes exposure to debate topics across political, religious, ideological and/or cultural spectrums, reflecting the diversity of arguments found in society. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops skills in critical thinking, research and communication essential for professional, academic and/or civic life. Builds competence in evaluating arguments, analyzing evidence and presenting claims effectively to diverse audiences. Strengthens oral and written study of advocacy, responsive listening and adaptability in structured debate and informal discussion. Skills gained are directly relevant to law, politics, business, media, public policy and other areas where persuasive communication and sound reasoning are central. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday argument practices differ from structured approaches developed in debate and communication studies. Expands understanding of argument as more than personal opinion, showing how reasoning, evidence and ethical standards shape persuasion. Explores frameworks for evaluating arguments across different contexts, including individual decision-making, group deliberation, political campaigns and/or public debates. Highlights how cultural values and ideological perspectives influence the ways arguments are constructed and received. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include foundations of argument and debate; analysis of debate propositions; evaluation of evidence and proof; construction of affirmative and negative cases; cross-examination and refutation; ethical and cultural considerations in argument; listening and evaluation; debate as a form of public speaking; formats in academic, political and public debates. Course materials and debate topics may address diverse and sometimes controversial issues, reflecting the range of perspectives present in public discourse.

subject: COMM

Considers how independent voices create, challenge and reshape narratives in communities and public discourse. Attention to the relationship between personal voice, creativity and professional practice, as well as to issues of credibility, trust, ethics and representation. Highlights how independent media can be both a space of empowerment and a site of contestation. Highlights how digital platforms amplify personal, cultural and political voices, while also raising ethical and practical challenges. Highlights how identity, power and representation shape media production and reception. Develops understanding of the opportunities and limits of independent communication in contemporary society. Explores the opportunities and challenges presented by changes in the media landscape. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of blogs, podcasts, video and social media platforms; exploration of digital storytelling and creative expression; consideration of ethics, representation and credibility in independent media; analysis of activism, politics and identity as expressed through digital platforms; evaluation of how independent voices influence communities, industries and public life. Course applications may draw on popular culture, current events and emerging issues. Discussions may also engage with controversial or contested topics, reflecting the role of independent media in addressing subjects that shape public dialogue. Cross-listed with JOUR 250.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Media Literacy in the Digital Age. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores mass media as a form of communication across cultural, political and creative contexts. Examines how news media, podcasts, social media, video, television and advertising are used to inform, persuade, critique and/or tell stories. Analyzes source, audience, message design and the relationship between medium and purpose. Examines how information, misinformation and disinformation spreads, developing skills and techniques for assessing credibility and verifying sources. Includes engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may arise through topics connected to politics, culture, ethics and/or lived experience. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Prepares for advanced academic study in communication, media studies, journalism and related fields where digital fluency and critical media analysis are expected. Promotes awareness of how traditional media and independent media practices can contribute to civic discourse, cultural participation and emerging communication markets. Encourages media literacy in both communication careers and everyday life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how new media platforms differ from legacy communication systems in structure, purpose and power. Highlights the role of individual voice, audience interaction and platform design in shaping meaning and influence. Encourages recognition that public communication through digital media may challenge assumptions about authority, expertise and representation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis or creation of blogs, podcasts, social media campaigns, digital storytelling or multimedia commentary; exploration of how mass media engage politics, identity, culture and public issues; study of persuasion, narrative, audience engagement and message strategy in digital contexts. Assignments may involve analysis, production or both, depending on the instructor’s approach. Course materials may involve perspectives or content reflecting varied experiences, beliefs and interpretations encountered in contemporary media environments. Cross-listed with JOUR 255.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication, Religion and the Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of art and religion as forms of communication, with attention to how visual and artistic expression conveys meaning across cultures and traditions. Surveys artistic and media practices in religious and secular contexts, considering how aesthetics mediate religious experience and shape public understanding. Examines the role of art in supporting, questioning and/or challenging religious and social perspectives. Focus on interpretation and critique and dialogue of artifacts across diverse traditions, including attention to issues of pluralism, inequality, power, class and/or representation. Includes engagement with perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in interpreting and discussing art and religion across diverse cultural and historical contexts. Builds skills for engaging respectfully with differences in belief, practice and/or worldview. Strengthens intercultural awareness, critical thinking and creative communication skills, which can be applied to dialogue across divisions in civic, professional and interpersonal settings. Enhances understanding of how art and media shape public awareness of religion and contributes to broader conversations about meaning, identity and social conflict. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how the study of art and religion in communication differs from devotional or confessional approaches. Expands understanding of religion as a cultural and communicative practice shaped by history, power and interpretation. Highlights how art functions not only to express belief but also to question, challenge or reframe religious ideas. Introduces perspectives that encourage critical analysis of how religion and art intersect with broader cultural, social and/or political contexts. Emphasizes reflection on pluralism and contested meanings, deepening awareness of how religion and art shape, and are shaped by, the wider human experience. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication, art and religion as interrelated cultural practices; exploration of how visual and artistic forms convey meaning within Christianity, Buddhism, Islam, secular humanism and other traditions; consideration of iconoclasm, pluralism and the role of art in shaping or challenging belief and practices; attention to aesthetics, power, inequality and representation in religious and secular contexts. Course materials may also engage with the profane or the obscene when relevant to understanding how religion, art and communication define, resist and/or reframe cultural boundaries. Content may include perspectives that are unfamiliar, contested or controversial, reflecting the diversity of ways art and religion intersect in public life. Cross-listed with RELS 257.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Introduction to Social Media. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores social media as a communication environment shaped by technology, audience, participation and platform design. Surveys major platforms, concepts and theories used to understand how individuals, organizations and communities create, share and interpret digital content. Examines how social media intersects with journalism, marketing, activism, entertainment and/or everyday communication. Considers how digital communication practices reflect and influence public discourse, society and culture. Engagement with real-world examples may involve topics connected to politics, religion, identity, ethics and/or lived experiences. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices connected to media industries, strategic messaging, journalism, advertising, nonprofit work, politics and other forms of public communication. Involves skills relevant to content creation, audience analysis, audience engagement, platform analysis and communication strategy. Connects to professional and academic paths in media, communication, journalism, marketing, public affairs and digital culture. Supports academic preparation to analyze ways social media shapes institutional messaging, cultural participation, community formation and civic dialogue. Develops applied skill in using social media strategically within entrepreneurial, organizational or community campaign contexts. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication via social media platforms differs from legacy media in participation, access and influence. Explores communication theories and strategies underpinning social media communication. Highlights tensions involving credibility, persuasion, privacy, visibility and/or identity in digital environments. Builds understanding of how platforms shape perception, behavior and communication norms in ways that are not always immediately visible. Supports informed assessment of one’s own media usage patterns and communication practices as case material for analysis. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication theories, platform histories and digital ecosystems; analysis of messaging strategies and audience behavior; consideration of digital identity, participation and online communities; exploration of ethics, credibility, privacy, representation and influence in online environments; examination of how platforms shape visibility, participation and public discourse; study of consent, branding, advocacy, journalism and influencer practices; comparison of interactive and traditional media. Course materials may reflect varied perspectives and examples from professional, cross-cultural and/or global contexts. Cross-listed with JOUR 275.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Careers in Communication and Journalism. (1-0). Credit 1. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores fields and pathways in journalism, media and communication-related professions. Considers how professional interests, strengths and personality align with opportunities in media, public communication, journalism, strategic communication, digital platforms and related industries. Addresses foundational practices in networking, resume-writing, application material preparation, informational interviewing and digital presence. Includes exposure to campus resources and career planning tools. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds awareness of workforce expectations and industry pathways across communication-related professions. Introduces practical strategies for pursuing careers in media, advocacy, corporate communication, public affairs or related sectors. Assists in translation of classroom knowledge in securing internships, applied experience and long-term professional development opportunities. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication careers vary in purpose, setting and expectation. Highlights differences between common assumptions about media or communication work and the range of roles that exist across industries. Builds awareness of how skills, identity, professionalism and context shape access to and participation in communication fields. Provides support to students transferring into CMJR, promoting academic success and facilitating engagement with campus resources and communities. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include identification of career interests and strengths; exploration of communication professions and industries; development of application materials; digital portfolios and networking strategies; informational interviewing; engagement with professional resources and advising. Course activities may reference academic planning, campus involvement, workplace preparation and/or communications-specific career development. Must be taken on a satisfactory/unsatisfactory basis. Cross-listed with JOUR 280.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Rhetorical Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces major traditions of rhetorical theory from antiquity to the present, examining how thinkers have defined persuasion, argument and public influence across changing political and cultural contexts. Considers contributions from figures across historical and contemporary contexts and how they theorize the role of rhetoric to shape civic life, challenge authority and/or construct knowledge. Focuses on how rhetorical theories and practices emerge in moments of conflict, uncertainty and social change. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Provides grounding in the foundations of rhetorical theory, building academic preparation for advanced study in rhetoric, political communication, law, public affairs and media criticism. Builds familiarity with frameworks widely used in speechwriting, advocacy, leadership communication and public reasoning. Supports professional and civic participation by clarifying how arguments gain legitimacy, how authority is constructed and how persuasive strategies function across traditions and institutions. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how rhetoric is more than just “style” or manipulation by revealing its role in philosophy, religion, science and governance. Reveals how foundational ideas such as reason, justice, virtue and truth were articulated through rhetorical means. Highlights how rhetorical theory reflects its time and audience, prompting reflection on how present-day communication inherits past assumptions about credibility, character and civic participation. TOPICS AND THEMES. Topics may include the study of classical Greek and Roman rhetoric, including persuasion, ethos and civic speech; consideration of Enlightenment and revolutionary rhetoric in the formation of democratic publics; examination of modern/contemporary rhetorical theories; exploration of rhetoric as epistemology — how discourse shapes truth, identity and/or power. Course material may include texts addressing religion, gender, sexuality, class, race, nationality and/or ideology, reflecting the diverse contexts of how rhetorical traditions have been developed and contested. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication and Data Visualization. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores data as a form of communication and examines how information is interpreted, visualized and presented for different audiences and purposes. Emphasizes data storytelling as both an analytical and narrative practice, focusing on how visual choices shape understanding. Considers visualization designs that use data to inform, explain, persuade and/or support decision-making, using tools such as Excel and R. Addresses principles of visual perception, evidence-based messaging and interpretation of qualitative data and quantitative analyses, including descriptive and inferential statistics. Considers how visual choices, context and audience shape meaning in visual communication. Coursework may involve analysis, critique and/or development of data-driven messages in digital or visual formats. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds data visualization skills relevant to journalism, strategic messaging, marketing, public affairs, organizational communication, media production, research presentation and political advocacy. Builds capacity to interpret data, build visual explanations and representations and present insights in accessible formats. Supports effectiveness in academic and professional contexts where evidence, visualization and communication intersect. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how data gain meaning through interpretation, framing and visual design. Highlights the difference between raw information and communicative impact. Encourages attention to credibility, context and the persuasive or explanatory use of visualized evidence. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study and critique of data visualizations; analysis of how charts, maps, dashboards, infographics or interactive visuals communicate meaning; consideration of audience adaptation, ethics, representation or narrative framing; exploration of digital storytelling strategies in data communication, including how sequencing, emphasis and interactivity guide interpretation; consideration of persuasive and informative uses of data in media, public communication, organizational settings or digital platforms. Course content may involve real-world issues or case studies that reflect diverse perspectives or public debate. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with JOUR 305.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Grade of B or better in COMM 275, COMM 323, or JOUR 200; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Digital Communication Analytics and Metrics. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of digital communication, data and the use of analytics to generate insight, evaluate communication strategies and inform decision-making. Examines techniques for extracting and interpreting information from websites, social media platforms and/or digital campaigns. Examines how data are used to assess audience behavior, platform performance, search engine optimization, message reach, engagement and/or return on investment. Considers how digital tactics connect across marketing, digital media platforms and communication research. Draws attention to the role of data in strategic planning. Course concepts are illustrated with examples that may involve digital communication in organizational, commercial, journalistic, political and/or nonprofit contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Promotes workforce preparation for careers in strategic communication, public relations, advertising, journalism, marketing, audience research and digital media. Advances understanding and skills related to interpreting performance metrics, applying measurement models and using analytics to support campaigns, outreach, reporting and/or organizational decision-making. Supports academic and professional work in areas where communication effectiveness, audience insight and data-informed planning intersect. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies the role of analytics in shaping communication strategy, storytelling and/or organizational decision-making. Highlights the difference between data collection and meaningful interpretation. Builds recognition of how digital communication practices intersect with privacy expectations, ethical obligations and the constraints of data tracking and measurement. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of web traffic, audience demographics and user behavior; study of paid, earned and owned media metrics; consideration of measurement models, platform dashboards and optimization tactics; exploration of data-driven decision-making, campaign evaluation, content performance, randomized field experiment and competitive research. Course examples may involve sectors such as journalism, marketing, nonprofit advocacy, strategic communication and/or politics, reflecting the varied uses of digital analytics in public communication. Prerequisites: Grade of B or better in COMM 275, COMM 323, or JOUR 200; junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with JOUR 306.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Theories of Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores major theoretical approaches to human communication, focusing on how communication theory explains language and symbol use, rhetoric, interpersonal interaction, small group and organizational dynamics, persuasion and/or media/technological influence. Examines humanistic, social scientific and/or critical theoretical traditions in communication studies. Explores ways theories of communication help to explain what communication is, how it functions and why it matters in different settings. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in communication and related fields. Provides a foundation for understanding how theories inform research, professional communication strategies, media practices and organizational decision-making. Develops transferable skills in analytical reasoning, interpretation of communication processes and application of abstract concepts to real-world situations. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how theoretical perspectives may differ from everyday assumptions about communication. Demonstrates how concepts such as persuasion, meaning-making and media influence can be examined through different theoretical frameworks, offering distinct insights and applications. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of interpersonal communication theories; analysis of language and symbol use; examination of group and organizational interaction; consideration of persuasion and influence; exploration of media and technology’s role in communication; comparison of interpretive and scientific approaches to theory. Course content may reference diverse cultural, social and/or institutional contexts to illustrate how communication theories operate in practice. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification, or approval of instructor.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: 6 hours of MATH 140, MATH 142, MATH 151, MATH 152, PHIL 240 or STAT 201.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Research Methods in Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores major approaches to studying communication through empirical methods, with an emphasis on hands-on learning and research-by-doing. Focuses on how researchers formulate questions, select appropriate methods and collect and analyze data. Examines quantitative and qualitative approaches to studying messages, media, audiences and social interaction. Builds foundations in the application of specific research methods commonly used in the communication discipline such as surveys, experiments, content analysis, in-depth interviews, focus groups and rhetorical analysis. Incorporates consideration of research design, sampling, measurement, ethics, basic data analysis and interpretation across communication contexts. Emphasizes how different methods generate different types of insight and evidence. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects directly to fields that rely on evidence-based communication research, including media studies, public relations, organizational communication, health communication, audience analytics and strategic messaging. Involves practices used in academic research, market research, program evaluation and professional data analysis. Builds competencies valued in communication industries and graduate study, including research literacy, analytical reasoning, data interpretation and methodological decision-making. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how research in communication differs from everyday opinion, anecdote and assumptions. Considers how different research methods generate different kinds of evidence and how those differences shape interpretation and conclusion. Encourages reflection on the limits, possibilities and ethics of studying communication in human and mediated contexts. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of research questions and hypotheses; analysis of quantitative methods such as surveys, experiments or content analysis; consideration of qualitative and interpretive approaches such as interviews, focus groups or ethnography; exploration of sampling, measurement, validity, reliability, data collection and interpretation. Applications may draw from interpersonal, organizational, media, digital, political and/or critical/cultural communication contexts. Prerequisites: 6 hours of MATH 140, MATH 142, MATH 151, MATH 152, PHIL 240 or STAT 201.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication Intervention. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of communication interventions designed to create change at individual, interpersonal, organizational and/or community levels. Examines theories and models used to influence behavior, participation and decision-making in such contexts as voting, purchasing, membership, health campaigns and training. Focus on how communication strategies are designed, implemented and assessed using social science-based approaches. Addresses message design, needs assessment, change models, persuasion processes and evaluation of outcomes. Course work may involve application of theories to real and/or hypothetical cases. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops intervention skills relevant to professional practice in organizational communication, health communication, training and development, leadership, consulting, public relations, marketing and civic or community initiatives. Involves skills tied to planning campaigns, designing persuasive messaging, conducting needs assessments and evaluating effectiveness of communication-based interventions. Aligns with academic and applied fields that use communication to facilitate change within individuals, institutions, communities and public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how communication functions not only as information delivery but as a strategic tool for intervention and influence. Highlights the role theory can play explaining how and why change occurs. Explores the complex factors to consider in designing effective communication interventions, as well as the need to ground strategies in research-based models rather than assumptions. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of intervention theories and models; analysis of change strategies across individual, group, organizational and community contexts; consideration of message design, persuasion and implementation; exploration of needs assessment, behavior change frameworks, action research, dialogic approaches, training design and evaluation models. Examples may draw from campaigns, organizations, communities, public initiatives and/or social or institutional problem-solving. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Interpersonal Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines key concepts and theories for understanding how people create, maintain and sometimes challenge relationships through communication. Considers person-to-person and online interaction, including perception, attraction, self-disclosure, listening and/or conflict management. Explores communication across interpersonal differences such as professional and social roles, class, age, ability, gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, nationality and religion. Examines practices for analyzing interpersonal communication through research and theory. Course materials may include consideration of diverse perspectives and examples of communication as both productive and destructive, in face-to-face and online contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds skills for effective interaction in personal, professional and civic settings. Develops tools for effective listening, conflict management and resolution and adapting to others from diverse backgrounds and perspectives. Supports understanding of how interpersonal communication influences health, well-being and quality of life. Builds academic preparation for advanced study and workforce preparation for careers requiring teamwork, leadership and strong relational and collaborative competence. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday ideas about relationships and communication may differ from research-based perspectives. Considers ways that listening involves more than paying attention, that conflict can strengthen as well as weaken relationships and reasons disclosure and trust do not always follow predictable stages. Builds recognition of how identity, culture and context shape meaningful interactions, showing ways communication approaches that seem natural in one setting may be interpreted differently or counter-productively in another. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of perception, attraction, self-disclosure, listening and conflict management; study of interaction patterns and stages in relationship development; analysis of communication across interpersonal dimensions such as gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, ability, nationality and religion; consideration of productive and destructive aspects of communication; application of interpersonal theory to face-to-face and online contexts, including social media. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

Surveys foundational theories and contemporary perspectives on how communication influences organizing, including attention to practices associated with collective identity-building, leadership, decision-making, culture, power, technology use and/or change. Examines how communication enables coordination across teams and influences how people experience belonging, authority or conflict in organizational life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce preparation for professional contexts where collaboration, leadership and organizational activities depend on communication across roles, departments and demographic or cultural differences. Examples or case discussions may draw from corporate, governmental, nonprofit, academic and/or community contexts. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Strategic Communication Case Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how communication strategies are developed to align stakeholder needs with organizational goals within public environments. Considers planning models, message design, effective tactics, channel selection, evaluation, budgeting and collaboration with community or client partners. Emphasizes analysis, problem-solving and adaptation of communication practices across professional, nonprofit and/or civic contexts. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects strategic communication to professional contexts, such as public relations, integrated marketing communication, nonprofit campaigns and initiatives, branding, media production and/or organizational communication. Develops skills and foundations relevant to situation, organization, and stakeholder analysis, campaign planning, message development, collaboration with stakeholders and applied research. Aligns with marketplace settings where communication is used to shape perception, coordinate action and address public needs or organizational challenges. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how strategic communication differs from general messaging, sales or promotion. Highlights the role of planning, research and ethics in shaping communication outcomes. Encourages reflection on how strategy must adjust to different audiences, purposes and constraints, rather than relying on a single model or platform. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include case analysis of campaigns; study of stakeholder identification, goals and messaging; application of communication research; media writing and visual communication; channel strategy; budgeting, collaboration with organizations; evaluation and adaptation of communication plans. Course projects or examples may involve nonprofit, corporate, governmental or community settings and may draw on diverse perspectives and public issues. prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication Leadership and Conflict Management. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines leadership and conflict through a communication lens. Focuses on how people create shared understandings of what “counts” as leadership and how leaders manage tensions and conflicts as they seek to exert influence, coordinate collaborative efforts and mobilize collective action. Considers conflict as a communicative phenomenon in interpersonal, group, organizational and societal settings. Emphasizes how different meanings of leadership and conflict are constructed, contested and transformed through communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Connects to professional, organizational, civic and community contexts where leadership and conflict management are central to collaboration and decision-making. Relevant to careers involving teamwork, supervision, facilitation, advocacy, public affairs, consultation and organizational development. Addresses communication practices used to build credibility, respond to tension, coordinate diverse perspectives and guide collective problem solving. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how leadership is enacted through communication rather than position or personality. Highlights the inevitability of conflict in common leadership contexts and the range of communicative responses it can elicit. Encourages analysis of how power, relationships and context shape approaches to collaboration and disagreement. Differentiates between constructive and destructive communication patterns in navigating conflict. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of leadership theories as communication phenomena; analysis of dialogue, negotiation and mediation; examination of conflict in interpersonal, group, organizational and public settings; systemic and constructionist approaches to collaboration; use of symbols in leadership communication; management of difference in diverse teams and communities. Examples may address professional, civic, institutional and/or societal contexts in which leadership communication shapes outcomes and relationships. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Persuasion. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of persuasive communication across interpersonal, group, organizational and public contexts. Examination of how messages influence beliefs, attitudes and behavior through rhetorical, psychological and social processes. Focus on audience analysis, source credibility, language, nonverbal influence, motivational appeals, ethics and theories of attitude change. Includes engagement with real-world persuasive contexts that may involve topics and examples that are politically, culturally and/or socially contested, examined for the purpose of understanding how persuasive communication operates. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applicable to communication work in media, health, politics, marketing, advocacy, leadership and organizational contexts. Informs message design, audience adaptation and analysis of influence strategies across professional and public settings. Relevant to professional fields that require reasoning, strategic communication and interpretation of persuasive efforts in civic, commercial or interpersonal life. Builds awareness of how persuasion operates in campaigns, advertising, negotiations and/or community outreach. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how persuasion involves more than argument or performance, incorporating credibility, motivation, perception, emotion and context. Distinguishes between influence, coercion, propaganda and ethical advocacy. Highlights how attitudes and judgments are shaped by message design, social norms, personal experience and situational factors. Encourages reflection on how persuasive communication functions within everyday decision-making and public discourse. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of persuasive theories; study of attitudes and attitude change; credibility and message design; emotional and motivational appeals; ethical considerations in persuasion; influence in interpersonal, group and mediated settings; language, nonverbal strategies and message framing; resistance, compliance, refutation and evaluation of persuasive claims. Course examples may involve public health messaging, political communication, advertising, advocacy campaigns and/or other areas where the use of persuasive strategies is debated or contested. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication in a Diverse World. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores key concepts and theories for understanding how communication both reflects and shapes diversity in today’s world. Students study the mutual constitution of culture and communication, or the idea that communication practices both shape culture and are shaped by it. Examines one or more dimensions of identity, including gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, ability, nationality and religion, and how these dimensions affect communication across personal, organizational, public and/or other contexts. Includes practice in analyzing communication through critical and cultural perspectives. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Equips students with tools to navigate communication in diverse personal, professional and civic settings. Concepts and perspectives studied here apply directly to working in multicultural teams, exercising inclusive leadership and adapting to varied audiences in workplace and public contexts. Beyond career preparation, the course fosters critical awareness of how communication practices shape social realities, offering frameworks for lifelong learning, responsible citizenship and public/community engagement. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how terms such as culture, identity and diversity are defined within communication research and scholarly traditions, which may differ from everyday usage. Demonstrates how these concepts shape interaction, expectations and interpretation, revealing contexts in which cultural difference functions as a central dimension of communicative practice. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include exploration of how communication reflects and shapes cultural difference; study of identity across dimensions such as gender, race, ethnicity, sexuality, social class, ability, nationality and/or religion; analysis of how communication practices can reinforce or challenge inequity; consideration of communication across interpersonal, organizational and/or public contexts; introduction to critical and cultural perspectives on communication and diversity. Course may include content that is controversial or contested, as relevant to examining the ways differences in belief, perspective and lived experience shape communication practices. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Media Industries. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the structures, economics and regulation of media industries across sectors such as film, television, music, publishing, video games, streaming and/or digital platforms. Examines how content is produced, financed, distributed and governed within commercial, public and hybrid systems. Considers trends in media ownership, labor practices, media convergence, globalization, audience markets and/or media policy. Attention to the roles of technology, culture and/or law in shaping how media industries operate. Course material may engage with real-world issues involving politics, regulation, representation and/or controversy, as relevant to understanding industry practices. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to careers in media production, media law and policy, journalism, strategic communication, entertainment management, marketing, publishing and digital platforms. Informs understanding of how media businesses make decisions, respond to regulatory pressures and adapt to changing technologies and audiences. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, business, law and policy. Useful for those navigating or analyzing industries shaped by ownership structures, market forces and cultural influence. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how media industries function beyond consumption and cultural familiarity. Highlights the interplay of economic interests, creative labor, technology and public policy. Encourages recognition of the power dynamics and institutional processes that shape media access, visibility and innovation. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of media ownership and consolidation; production, distribution and exhibition systems; financing models and supply-chain relations; regulation and public policy; labor and creative work; technology and convergence; niche and mass markets; globalization and cultural circulation; media ethics and advocacy. prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Explores how media and technology represent, reinforce and challenge ideas about identity, power and social differences. Examines theories of communication and culture to understand how media shape and are shaped by beliefs about race, gender, class, sexuality, ability, nationality and/or religion. Considers how communication practices construct and contest meanings of belonging, visibility and participation. Engagement with real-world issues and diverse perspectives may involve topics that are culturally, politically and/or socially sensitive, discussed for the purpose of academic analysis and critical understanding. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Provides foundations for future professionals in journalism, digital media, strategic communication, public advocacy and related fields to anticipate audience response, avoid misrepresentation and build public trust. Builds transferable skills in media literacy, cultural analysis and ethical communication across professional and civic settings. Supports excellence in leadership and teamwork in diverse workplaces by considering how identity and difference influence communication dynamics. Supports advanced study in media studies, communication, cultural studies and related areas concerned with diversity and representation. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how cultural identities and media forms are interdependent, showing how meaning, power and visibility are negotiated through communication. Encourages reflection on the social roles of media institutions, creators and audiences in shaping public discourse and cultural imagination. Highlights the importance of dialogue, critical awareness and informed engagement in multicultural and mediated environments. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include representation and ideology in film, television, music and digital platforms; intersectionality and social identity; media and power; race, gender and sexuality in cultural production; class, globalization and inequality; disability and visibility; fandom, subcultures and participatory media; and contemporary debates around bias, equity and inclusion. Course material may include media content addressing real-world controversies or differing viewpoints, as relevant to understanding media, culture and identity. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with JOUR 346.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Theories of Mediated Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores theoretical approaches to understanding how media shapes and is shaped by communication, perception, multiple axes of social identity and/or social behavior. Surveys models of media processes and effects, including cognitive, behavioral and sociocultural perspectives. Examines how media theory explains influence, interpretation and interaction across traditional and digital platforms. Emphasizes how theories function within social-scientific research and guide analysis of mediated experience. Discussion may include contemporary issues and/or case studies involving controversial or sensitive topics, addressed for purposes of theoretical and empirical understanding. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to careers in media research, strategic communication, journalism, digital analytics and audience engagement. Builds knowledge of how theoretical frameworks support evidence-based reasoning, message design and interpretation, and media strategy. Contributes to professional and academic preparation in fields that rely on understanding media processes, including marketing, public relations, public policy, journalism and communication science. Supports civic literacy by exploring how mediated communication might influence opinion, participation and information exchange. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how media theory connects abstract ideas with empirical study, distinguishing theoretical explanation from personal impression or political interpretation. Highlights how systematic approaches reveal the mechanisms and conditions under which media affect individuals and society. Encourages appreciation of theory as a tool for interpreting complexity, rather than prescribing belief or ideology. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of major traditions and frameworks explaining how media shape perception, thought, multiple axes of social identity and social experience; examination of theories of media effects, audience behavior and communication influence; exploration of how theory functions in research, guiding explanation, prediction and interpretation across print, broadcast, digital and networked media. Course material may address real-world examples and controversies involving technology, news, politics or entertainment, as relevant to understanding how communication theories explain mediated processes and effects. Equips students with tools for working with global media across cultural differences. Builds skills in evaluating international news, identifying propaganda and disinformation and applying ethical standards across cultures. Prepares students for careers in journalism, public affairs and related fields requiring cross-cultural awareness and media literacy. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Develops understandings of press freedom, news values and global information flows, recognizing that media systems operate within distinct political, cultural and economic contexts; exploring how interconnected stories affecting different countries and regions have developed through globalization and social media. May include exploration of comparative media systems; study of world news flows and international reporting; press freedom, censorship and ethics; political propaganda, public diplomacy and soft power; international advertising and global news cultures; impact of digital technologies, social media and generative AI; challenges of disinformation and “fake news” in global communication. Focuses on how communication shapes health beliefs, behaviors and outcomes in clinical, community and/or policy settings. Builds competence in applying communication strategies to health-related issues across professional, civic and personal life. Prepares for advanced study for roles in organizations and industries where health communication is central. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how everyday views of health and illness differ from those developed through research and cultural analysis. Studies ways health communication involves not only the exchange of information but also negotiation of meaning, culture and/or power. Considers how communication practices influence perceptions of wellness, treatment and/or health equity. Course may involve engagement with sensitive topics such as illness, mortality, mental health, reproductive health and public health controversies. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of patient-provider communication, organizational communication in health care systems and communication in health policy and study of advocacy; exploration of health campaigns, media representations and the use of technology and social media in promoting health; consideration of social support, cultural perspectives on health and illness and the role of communication in shaping individual and collective health outcomes.
