prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Media Audiences. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of media audiences across empirical and interpretive research traditions. Examines how audiences are measured, targeted, persuaded, entertained and/or mobilized in effects-based frameworks. Considers how audiences might interpret, resist or rework media. Explores audience engagement with such content as news, entertainment, political communication, health messaging and advertising. Addresses how age, identity, ideology and/or context shape audience reception and response. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages practices central to media strategy, public communication, digital analytics, outreach and message design. Builds understanding of how audiences are researched, segmented and addressed in journalism, advertising, public health, politics, entertainment and digital media industries. Supports academic preparation in media effects theory, reception theory and communication research. Enhances awareness of how audience behavior shapes public discourse. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Complicates everyday assumptions that audiences passively receive media or predictably react to it. Highlights how persuasion and interpretation emerge through interaction between media content, audience predispositions and/or social contexts. Emphasizes that the study of mass media audiences requires attention to both influence and agency, data, and context. TOPICS AND THEMES. Study of audience behavior across news, entertainment, advertising and/or digital platforms; examination of media effects models, interpretive reception theories and audience participation logics; analysis of how audiences attend, interpret, resist or repurpose media content; consideration of political messaging, health campaigns, consumer persuasion, fandom and/or public controversy as sites for audience analysis. Examples may include media involving politics, public health, identity or moral debate when relevant to understanding media audiences. Course material may reference real-world cases or contested media environments for the purpose of analysis. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Gender, Race and Media. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how gender, race, sexuality, ethnicity and related identities are produced, represented, negotiated, contested, consumed and/or performed in relation to media. Explores contributions of historically marginalized groups to media production, alongside analysis of how these groups have been portrayed as characters, audiences, communities and/or target markets. Focuses on media as a site of competing commercial, cultural, political, satirical and/or resistance narratives, rather than as a single, unified voice. Emphasizes critical interpretation of media texts and systems, while allowing space for multiple viewpoints and interpretations. Course material may include historical and contemporary examples that reflect both progress and controversy, analyzed for their cultural and communicative significance. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages issues central to media literacy, political economy, representation and audience awareness in contemporary communication industries. Builds recognition of the ways portrayals of gender and race shape perception, credibility and/or trust in journalism, entertainment, advertising, representatives, community and public communication. Supports careers in communication, media industries, public relations, education, nonprofit work and leadership roles where navigating diverse audiences is essential. Supports informed decision-making in professional and civic contexts by highlighting how media representations influence identity, inclusion and public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies that studying media portrayals of gender and race is not limited to celebration or criticism but involves examining how representation functions within broader cultural, social, economic, political and/or institutional systems. Illustrates how media are grounded in economies of production, representation and consumption across platforms, products and pipelines. Considers ways media might be empowering, stereotypical, commercial and/or transformative, depending on context, audience and community. Promotes awareness that interpretations of media content may differ across social, cultural and/or generational perspectives and that disagreement over meaning is part of scholarly analysis rather than a flaw in the material. Normalizes engagement with sensitive or contested topics as a means of understanding how media both reflect and shape public life. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of media across film, television, news, advertising, music and digital platforms through production, representation and consumption; analysis of gender, race, ethnicity and intersectional identities in historical and contemporary contexts; consideration of media production practices, audience reception and the economic and institutional forces shaping representation; examination of stereotypes, invisibility, empowerment narratives and commercialized identity; discussion of how media both reinforce and challenge social norms related to power, privilege and belonging. Course material may include content that reflects real-world disparities or conflicting viewpoints. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with WGST 407.

Examines popular music as a form of communication shaped by technology, industry structures and cultural context. Traces how radio broadcasting, recording formats and digital platforms influence music creation, distribution and listening practices. Considers music as both entertainment and public discourse, attending to how artists, audiences and institutions construct meaning through sound, performance and/or media presence. Engagement with music connected to politics, commerce, identity or ethics may occur for the purpose of understanding communication processes. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens the ability to recognize how audio is used in journalism, marketing and civic communication to guide emotion and interpretation. Supports preparation for careers in media industries, music journalism, broadcasting, content strategy, audience analysis and arts promotion. Enhances critical and professional awareness of how music circulates in commercial and public life, informing work in creative industries, cultural analysis and public communication. Provides academic grounding for advanced study in media, culture, communication or popular music studies. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies distinctions between personal taste and scholarly analysis of music as communication. Encourages recognition of how technological formats, business models and cultural narratives influence what becomes popular, forgotten and/or controversial. Offers historical and structural context to familiar sounds, revealing music as shaped as much by systems as by creativity. TOPICS AND THEMES. Explores the study of motherhood as a cultural, social and communicative construct rather than a singular biological or personal identity. Examines how ideas about motherhood are created, reinforced or challenged through literature, film, popular media, digital media, political rhetoric, public policy, advertising, news, medical institutions and/or everyday discourse across different time periods and cultural contexts. Considers both idealized and marginalized portrayals, attending to such matters as gender, race, class, sexuality, ability and nation. Course material may include historical texts, contemporary examples, commentary and/or fictional representations. Content may include portrayals that are celebratory, critical or controversial, examined for purposes of interpretation. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds critical literacy for analyzing how cultural expectations shape perceptions of family, caregiving and social roles. Promotes awareness of how media narratives, cultural practices and public discourse influence policies, workplace norms, interpersonal expectations and public debates surrounding parenting, labor and care work. Supports workforce preparation in fields such as media, healthcare, public health, social work, policy development, education and public communication where sensitivity to diverse family structures and practices is essential. Enhances academic readiness for further study in rhetoric, gender studies, media studies and/or cultural studies. Encourages reflection on how public narratives about motherhood have evolved over time, affect social inclusion, policy decisions and public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how ideas about motherhood vary across cultures, eras, socio-economic groups and/or ideological perspectives, challenging assumptions of universality. Encourages recognition of both biological and socially constructed dimensions of maternal identity. Clarifies the difference between personal belief and cultural representation, prompting reflection on how individuals internalize or resist public narratives about care, responsibility and motherhood and how it may modify behavior. May include study of motherhood in literature, film, television, music, news, advertising, music and digital media; historical shifts in maternal ideals; feminist and anti-feminist discourses; motherhood and labor; political uses of maternal identity; race, class and marginalized motherhoods; disability and motherhood; reproductive technology and infertility narratives; representation of motherhood in children's literature and films, childfree identities and resistance to maternal norms. subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Representations of Motherhood. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of motherhood as a cultural, social and communicative construct rather than a singular biological or personal identity. Examines how ideas about motherhood are created, reinforced or challenged through literature, film, popular media, digital media, political rhetoric, public policy, advertising, news, medical institutions and/or everyday discourse across different time periods and cultural contexts. Considers both idealized and marginalized portrayals, attending to such matters as gender, race, class, sexuality, ability and nation. Course material may include historical texts, contemporary examples, commentary and/or fictional representations. Content may include portrayals that are celebratory, critical or controversial, examined for purposes of interpretation. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds critical literacy for analyzing how cultural expectations shape perceptions of family, caregiving and social roles. Promotes awareness of how media narratives, cultural practices and public discourse influence policies, workplace norms, interpersonal expectations and public debates surrounding parenting, labor and care work. Supports workforce preparation in fields such as media, healthcare, public health, social work, policy development, education and public communication where sensitivity to diverse family structures and practices is essential. Enhances academic readiness for further study in rhetoric, gender studies, media studies and/or cultural studies. Encourages reflection on how public narratives about motherhood have evolved over time, affect social inclusion, policy decisions and public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how ideas about motherhood vary across cultures, eras, socio-economic groups and/or ideological perspectives, challenging assumptions of universality. Encourages recognition of both biological and socially constructed dimensions of maternal identity. Clarifies the difference between personal belief and cultural representation, prompting reflection on how individuals internalize or resist public narratives about care, responsibility and motherhood and how it may modify behavior. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of motherhood in literature, film, television, music, news, advertising, music and digital media; historical shifts in maternal ideals; feminist and anti-feminist discourses; motherhood and labor; political uses of maternal identity; race, class and marginalized motherhoods; disability and motherhood; reproductive technology and infertility narratives; representation of motherhood in children's literature and films, childfree identities and resistance to maternal norms. Course material may involve emotional and sensitive content such as depictions of grief, trauma, marginalization or public controversy as relevant to understanding how motherhood is framed in culture. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with WGST 411.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: New Media and Civil Society. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how new media technologies shape civic participation, public discourse and/or social change across different political systems. Focus on communication practices in democratic, authoritarian and/or transitional societies. Considers how digital platforms enable organizing, surveillance, protest and/or community formation. Emphasizes theory-driven analysis of how online communication intersects with power, governance and collective life. Engagement with case studies from global and/or local contexts, including instances where media use is celebrated, contested or restricted. Course content and discussions may draw from different cultural or political contexts, including situations of disagreement or unrest, examined for purposes of understanding communication dynamics. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Emphasizes the role of digital communication in public affairs, advocacy, crisis response and institutional communication. Builds awareness of how media strategies function in political campaigns, nonprofit initiatives, international development and grassroots organizations. Supports professional work in public communication, policy analysis, journalism, technology sectors and civic engagement. Provides academic grounding for advanced study in media, politics, globalization or communication. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Complicates everyday assumptions about social media as inherently liberating or harmful. Encourages nuanced understanding of how digital tools can empower expression while reinforcing inequality or control. Highlights tensions between visibility and vulnerability, participation and manipulation. Models disagreement and controversy as part of understanding communication in public life rather than advocacy for a particular stance. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of civic participation and digital public spheres; analysis of social media activism, political protest and networked movements; examination of platform governance, censorship, surveillance and state messaging; consideration of misinformation, polarization, digital propaganda and extremist communication; exploration of online community-building, identity expression and digital inequalities; comparative perspectives across democratic, authoritarian and transitional societies. Course material may reference real-world cases involving political or cultural controversy, including but not limited to violence, hate speech or ideological conflict, for purposes of understanding how new media intersects with civic life, governance and social dynamics. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Rhetoric of Social Movements. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how social movements communicate their goals, identities and demands through speech, writing, media and/or performance. Analyzes rhetorical strategies used to mobilize supporters, challenge and create institutions and/or shape public perception in democratic and non-democratic contexts. Highlights how meaning, legitimacy and resistance are constructed through communication across different eras. Course content and discussion may reference contentious or opposing viewpoints for the purpose of understanding persuasive practice across specific topics. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds workforce preparation for careers involving advocacy, public communication, journalism, policy, law, nonprofit work or civic leadership; building understanding of how strategic messaging, storytelling and symbolism operate in public life. Enhances ability to gauge public sentiment, assess persuasive appeals and navigate disagreement in professional and community environments. Provides academic grounding for advanced study in rhetoric, media, political communication or social change. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals how definitions of “legitimate” protest or persuasion shift over time and across audiences. Considers why some tactics are celebrated while others are condemned and how public judgment is shaped by rhetoric, media coverage and institutional response. Considers social movements in terms of communication processes rather than moral binaries, revealing how communication strategies function across differing and at times opposing perspectives. TOPICS AND THEMES. Includes the study of how different groups across American history have advocated for or resisted changing the status quo. May include study of abolition, labor, suffrage, civil rights, feminist, Latina/o/x, Indigenous, environmental, gender justice, sexual rights, animal rights, student, anti-war, anti-racist, religious, conservative or populist social movements. Analysis of manifestos, speeches, protests, songs, visual rhetoric, digital campaigns or counter-movements. Exploration of strategies such as coalition-building, confrontation, satire, spectacle or moral appeal; consideration of state and media response to dissent, including repression, co-optation or commemoration. Course material may reference real-world cases involving social conflict or political controversy, examined analytically within an environment of respectful dialogue. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Topics in Rhetorical Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores rhetorical theory as a tool for analyzing persuasion, discourse and symbolic action across varied contexts. Considers how different theoretical frameworks clarify how language, images or performance influence belief, identity and/or judgment. Emphasizes application of theory to real-world communicative problems rather than abstract debate alone. Topics vary by instructor and may center on specific genres, intellectual traditions and/or individual theorists. Course content may involve materials ranging from public speeches to digital memes or popular media, examined for interpretive purposes rather than endorsement. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages communication practices relevant to leadership, advocacy, media analysis and civic or organizational strategy. Builds capacity to interpret persuasive discourse, assess rhetorical intent and/or articulate the assumptions embedded in public messages. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in rhetoric, media studies or communication theory. Contributes to professional roles that require message evaluation, argument framing or cultural awareness. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how rhetorical theory offers multiple lenses for interpreting the same message, highlighting ways meaning can be shaped by perspective rather than being fixed. Reveals how ethics, humor, philosophy, satire, activism and political discourse can operate as rhetorical strategies rather than solely as abstract ideas, entertainment or expressions of opinion. Allows engagement with unfamiliar or conflicting viewpoints as part of scholarly interpretation rather than persuasion. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of rhetorical problems such as nationalism, citizenship, identity or cultural critique; application of theories from classical, modern or contemporary traditions; examination of rhetoric as symbolic action in political, social, institutional or aesthetic contexts; exploration of discourse across spoken, written, visual or digital forms; analysis of how persuasion operates through appeals to truth, morality, identity, ritual or ideology. Specific course focus may vary by instructor, but all versions maintain emphasis on theory-driven inquiry. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Rhetoric of Television and Film. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores television and film as persuasive and symbolic communication. Examines rhetorical approaches to screen media, examining how narrative, genre, style, performance and/or visual form shape cultural meaning. Emphasizes close reading and critical interpretation of selected films, series and/or audiovisual texts. Course material may include popular, historical and/or controversial media — both domestic and international — analyzed for purposes of understanding communication strategy and effect. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops analytical and writing skills applicable to careers in media criticism, strategic communication, entertainment, journalism, advertising and social media. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in rhetoric, media studies, cultural analysis or related fields. Enhances civic awareness by strengthening the ability to assess how visual media influence identity, public opinion and debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how familiar entertainment texts function as arguments about identity, power, values or social norms. Reveals how meaning can emerge not only from content but also from framing, characterization and genre convention. Considers how television and film can provide evidence of changing cultural assumptions and act as resources for public imagination. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of genre and narrative structure; visual style and symbolism; representation of identity, morality or ideology; satire, parody and social commentary; industrial or historical context shaping production and reception; rhetorical frameworks drawn from classical, modern or contemporary theory. Course material may include programming or films involving violence, sexuality, religion and/or politically sensitive content, addressed for purposes of analysis within a respectful learning environment. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with FILM 445.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Visual Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of images as forms of communication across public, cultural and institutional contexts. Examines how visuals convey meaning, evoke emotion, construct identity and/or shape public perception. Considers photography, advertising, memorials, protest imagery, comics and/or other visual texts as rhetorical and symbolic acts. Course content and discussion may include real-world imagery that reflects social conflict, violence, inequality and/or sensitive subjects for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages visual literacy central to media work, journalism, advocacy, design and public communication. Builds recognition of how images influence opinion, memory and behavior across digital, institutional and interpersonal environments. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in media studies, rhetoric, journalism and cultural communication. Provides tools useful in professions requiring visual strategy, branding, storytelling or critical evaluation of mediated content. Contributes to civic awareness in a society where public debate increasingly occurs through images. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers ways visuals act not as neutral reflections of reality, but as constructed representations shaped by framing, selection and context. Highlights how different audiences interpret the same image differently, prompting reflection on perspective, bias and cultural positioning. Encourages recognition of how images communicate power, belonging and/or exclusion; sometimes subtly, sometimes provocatively. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of photography and public memory; advertising and consumer imagery; visual culture in politics, protest and activism; comics and graphic narrative; memorials and commemorative design; digital imagery, memes and viral circulation; depictions of identity, embodiment or community through visual media. May involve visual curation or creation of original materials. Course content may include powerful or controversial imagery, such as depictions of violence, tragedy, ideological symbolism or material some may consider profane or objectionable, examined for the purpose of informed and critical interpretation of visual communication. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Propaganda. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines propaganda as a strategic form of communication used across political, commercial and social contexts. Surveys historical and contemporary approaches to influencing mass audiences through language, imagery, narrative and emotion. Analyzes how persuasive appeals operate in mass media, digital platforms, public relations, advertising and/or institutional messaging. Considers distinctions between information, persuasion and manipulation, with attention to credibility, transparency and ethics. Content may include real-world messages that involve political conflict, sensitive beliefs or provocative imagery, studied for purposes of critical evaluation. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds analytical tools relevant to media literacy, strategic communication, journalism, marketing, political communication and public affairs. Supports preparation for roles requiring evaluation of persuasive messaging, audience response or ethical communication practices. Enhances readiness for advanced academic study in rhetoric, media studies or communication theory. Develops civic awareness by examining how influence can operate in democratic and non-democratic environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how propaganda differs from persuasion; critically engaging assumptions that it is always visible, extreme or partisan. Reveals how influence can work subtly through repetition, normalization and/or emotional framing. Considers how individuals evaluate messages, assign credibility and participate in communication systems, whether intentionally or unconsciously. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of propaganda techniques in politics, advertising, public relations and entertainment; analysis of historical and contemporary campaigns; exploration of visual, verbal and digital persuasion strategies; comparison of state, commercial and grassroots messaging; examination of credibility, emotion, repetition, symbolism and narrative in persuasive appeals. Course material may reference real-world examples involving political conflict, wartime messaging, extremist rhetoric or provocative imagery that is characteristic of contemporary propaganda and necessary for understanding its full range of expression in competitive and contentious public spheres. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Political Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of political communication as a central feature of democratic life. Examines how political messages are created and circulated across campaigns, institutions, movements, journalism and/or digital platforms. Focuses on how communication informs, persuades, mobilizes and/or divides public audiences, with attention to both effective strategy and ethical responsibility. Focuses on the role of political communication in shaping American political history. Course content may reference real-world political conflict, campaign rhetoric and controversial messaging strategies, examined for purposes of analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds civic literacy by strengthening the ability to recognize persuasive tactics, evaluate competing claims and interpret political messaging across media. Supports professional preparation for careers in public service, journalism, legal advocacy, strategic communication and civic leadership. Supports the ability for informed participation in elections, policy discussions or public dialogue. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Highlights how political discourse is shaped not only by logic and evidence but also by strategic goals, narrative, emotion, symbolism and framing. Explores how disagreement can function productively when guided by shared norms of deliberation, debate and mutual recognition. Develops awareness of how communication practices can either escalate division or foster understanding across political perspectives. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of campaign speeches, debates, advertisements and digital outreach; analysis of press and government relations, political journalism and media framing; exploration of grassroots mobilization, social movements and advocacy; comparison of institutional messaging across branches of government. Course material may engage contemporary political controversies or sharply divided viewpoints, addressed for purposes of understanding how communication shapes public judgment and democratic engagement. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication and Conflict. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of how communication practices shape the development, escalation and resolution of conflict across interpersonal, intergroup, organizational, family and/or public settings. Examines both theoretical frameworks and practical approaches to negotiation, mediation and/or facilitated dialogue. Course content may reference real-world disputes involving sensitive or emotionally charged situations, analyzed for communication insight. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds capacity for managing disagreement in personal, professional and civic environments. Strengthens competencies relevant to leadership, teamwork, client relations, human resources, counseling, public service and community engagement. Supports the ability to navigate high-stakes conversations, advocate constructively and participate effectively in decision-making processes. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers ways conflict is not always or necessarily destructive but also a potential site for clarification, innovation and relational growth. Explores how disagreement can surface unmet needs, reveal assumptions or prompt creative problem-solving when approached with strategic communication. Considers that managing conflict effectively requires awareness of both one’s own communicative choices and broader dynamics that shape interaction. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of interpersonal disputes; intergroup tensions and prejudices; workplace and organizational conflict; group decision-making dynamics; negotiation tactics and persuasive framing; mediation and third-party intervention; cultural and gender influences on conflict style; conflict in digital or mediated environments; reconciliation, apology and forgiveness. Case material may draw from personal, professional, civic or community contexts where disagreement plays a central role. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Media Campaigns. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Study of the principles and processes behind designing media campaigns across domains such as health, politics, human rights, advertising and/or the environment. Considers theory-driven planning, persuasive strategy, message execution and evaluation in mass and digital media contexts. Includes critical analysis of real-world campaign cases past and present alongside applied exercises in campaign design. Course content may feature campaign messages involving sensitive or controversial topics, examined to understand communication strategy. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Builds professional competencies relevant to advertising, strategic communication, public relations, health promotion, political advocacy and nonprofit outreach. Develops skills in message targeting, audience analysis, media planning and persuasive evaluation necessary for roles involving campaign development or consultancy. Supports preparation for advanced coursework in communication strategy and reinforces civic literacy by enhancing the ability to interpret and assess persuasive messaging encountered in public life. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how effective campaign messaging requires more than creativity, demanding ethical reasoning, audience insight, emotional appeal and theoretical grounding. Expands understanding of how persuasive appeals can operate differently across issues and identities, encouraging reflection on both intended and unintended effects. Frames media campaigns not only as tools for influence but also as cultural artifacts that reveal public priorities, fears and beliefs. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of campaign theory and history; message design and persuasive appeals; audience segmentation and targeting; media channel strategy across television, radio, print and digital platforms; evaluation of campaign effectiveness; social marketing and public health initiatives; political and issue advocacy; environmental and safety campaigns; crisis communication and public service announcements. Examples may draw from domestic and international cases and include campaign content that is emotional, graphic and/or politically charged, used for promoting informed, critical analysis. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Cultural Studies of Communication Technology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores how communication technologies shape and are shaped by culture, power and everyday life. Examines theories of technological change, media history and/or digital culture, including how new and emerging technologies are often met with complex social dilemmas. Draws on historical and contemporary examples to show how technologies such as telegraphy, television, social media and surveillance platforms carry assumptions about progress, identity, work and/or control. Course content may include cases involving political conflict, privacy concerns or online controversy, examined for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Supports professional preparation in fields concerned with media policy, strategic communication, digital storytelling, user experience, ethics or advocacy. Strengthens civic literacy by analyzing how technological narratives influence public trust, participation and responsibility. Builds awareness of how institutions, governments and communities negotiate access, autonomy and accountability in digital environments. Clarifies how contemporary debates over technology shape journalism, marketing, policy development, design practice and workplace communication. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Reveals ways technology is not always neutral but can be embedded within cultural expectations, economic systems and political values. Differentiates between everyday assumptions about innovation and scholarly approaches that analyze who benefits, who is excluded and how technological systems reinforce or redistribute power. Informs reflection on how personal devices, platforms and infrastructures can shape interaction, memory, identity and/or agency. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of technological determinism and cultural shaping of technology; utopian and dystopian narratives in media; infrastructures of communication throughout history; surveillance, data tracking and privacy; identity formation in digital communities; automation, labor and human-machine relations; digital inequality and access; governance of communication technologies in democratic and non-democratic contexts. Course materials may include historical case studies or contemporary examples involving censorship, exploitation and/or graphic or profane content as relevant to understanding communication and technology. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication and Video Games. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores video games as a field of communication study, examining their development as media industries, cultural practices and technological environments. Surveys scholarship on game studies history, video game production models, audience experiences and/or game design strategies. Investigates how gameplay involves storytelling, emotion, identity and interaction across different genres and mediums. Course material may include video games or related media that contain violence, mature content or controversial themes, examined for purposes of critical analysis and informed perspectives. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Engages skills applicable to media strategy, entertainment industries, marketing, game design, journalism and audience analysis. Builds familiarity with economic models, platform ecosystems and/or emerging markets surrounding digital entertainment. Supports academic preparation in communication, media studies, cultural studies and technology research. Enhances civic and cultural awareness by examining how interactive media shape norms, values and public debate. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how video games function not only as entertainment but also as sites of persuasion, identity performance, experimentation and cultural meaning. Examines distinctions between technological innovation and social consequences. Informs reflection on assumptions about players, genres, violence and/or interactivity by contrasting public debates with empirical and critical research. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of game history and platform evolution; analysis of development pipelines, publishing models and global industry structures; exploration of narrative design and emotional engagement; consideration of online communities, fandoms and participatory cultures; examination of regulation, monetization, labor, access and ethics. Course material may draw from games or case studies involving conflict, gender representation or political controversy as relevant to communication analysis. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Media, Health and Medicine. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines how health, illness and medical practice are represented across media environments, including news, social media, entertainment, advertising and/or public information campaigns. Analyzes how messages about bodies, risk, care, expertise and/or responsibility are constructed and circulated. Considers how media shape public expectations of patients, professionals and/or institutions. Course content may include real-world examples involving sensitive topics such as illness, disability, gender, sexuality, social class and/or race, examined for purposes of critical analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies to workforce settings in which effective communication about health is essential, including healthcare industries, public relations, nonprofit outreach, journalism and strategic communication. Supports academic preparation for advanced study in health communication, media studies and public health or policy. Strengthens civic media literacy by examining how health information and misinformation spread through media systems, institutional messaging and cultural narratives. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how portrayals of health are shaped not only by medical knowledge but also by narrative conventions, commercial pressures and/or cultural assumptions. Builds understanding of how media depictions of illness, caregiving and wellness can inform, inspire, mislead and/or stigmatize, depending on framing. Facilitates comparison between professional expertise and popular narratives to better understand how public perceptions of health are formed and challenged. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of medical dramas and documentaries; news coverage of disease outbreaks or medical innovation; health marketing and pharmaceutical advertising; public health campaigns and crisis communication; social media communities around wellness, disability or chronic illness; narratives of caregiving and recovery; depictions of healthcare providers and institutions. May include feminist and/or critical approaches to the intersections of health with topics like gender, race and sexuality. Course material may reference real-world historical and contemporary health controversies when useful for understanding communication processes. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Grade of B or better in COMM 275 or JOUR 275; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Advanced Social Media. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the strategic use of social media in professional, organizational and/or public communication contexts. Analyzes how platforms such as Instagram, TikTok, LinkedIn and/or X structure their visibility, engagement and audience expectations. Explores how organizations and individuals craft identity, manage interaction and respond to feedback across different platform cultures. Includes both critical evaluation of existing accounts and hands-on creation of posts, visuals and/or campaigns for specific purposes. Course material may reference real-world social media campaigns related to political, cultural and/or commercial controversy, examined for purposes of communication analysis. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Applies directly to careers in public relations, branding, journalism, advocacy, content strategy and digital marketing. Builds fluency in platform conventions, analytics, message design and audience targeting; skills applicable in both corporate and nonprofit communication roles. Supports academic growth in media analysis and prepares students for civic participation in increasingly networked communication environments. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how social media operates not only as a tool for promotion but as a space of negotiation between creators, institutions and publics. Highlights differences between personal posting, strategic messaging and algorithmic influence. Informs reflection on the challenges of authenticity, persuasion and accountability when communication is continuous, participatory and highly public. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include analysis of platform affordances and algorithmic logics; branding and identity construction; audience engagement strategies; visual and multimedia storytelling; analytics and performance metrics; influencer models and creator economies; platform policy, moderation and crisis response. Course examples may draw from corporate, political, entertainment, activist and/or nonprofit accounts. Content creation components may involve drafting posts, graphics, videos and/or campaign plans in response to simulated or real-world communication goals. Prerequisites: Grade of B or better in COMM 275 or JOUR 275; junior or senior classification.

subject: COMM
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Religious Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of religious communication in shaping public life through speeches, sermons, debates, campaigns and/or social movements. Considers how religious language, symbols and/or narratives influence cultural identity, moral reasoning and/or collective action. Surveys diverse approaches to studying religious communication, from historical traditions to contemporary debates, highlighting how meaning is constructed, contested and transformed in religious discourse. Considers interpretations of religious communication from multiple perspectives, fostering critical thinking. Explores a diverse range of scholarly frameworks, theories and methods employed in the academic study of religion and religious communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens transferable skills in critical thinking, interpretation and evaluation of persuasive messages in contexts ranging from personal dialogue to civic engagement. Enhances adaptability across diverse religious and cultural frameworks. Supports academic preparation for analyzing communication at the intersection of religion, culture and public life. Engages skills applicable to leadership, education, public study of advocacy and professional fields, when understanding religious perspectives and their influence is relevant. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how religious communication functions not only as a vehicle of belief but also as a force shaping history, politics and/or social change. Provides reflection on ways speeches, symbols and/or campaigns can both unite and divide, reinforcing traditions or sparking transformation. Provides frameworks for critical analysis of religious discourse from first-person and third-person perspectives. Highlights the interpretive challenges posed by pluralism, competing meanings and differing assumptions about authority, sacredness and public expression. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of religious speeches and sermons; debates over doctrine and belief; campaigns and movements shaped by religious rhetoric; analysis of religious symbolism and storytelling; exploration of the role of communication in sustaining or challenging religious traditions. Course materials may address diverse and sometimes controversial perspectives, reflecting the ways religious communication has influenced cultural identity, social conflict and civic life across history. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with RELS 480.

subject: COSC
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Life Cycle Assessment in Building Construction. (3-0). Credit 3. Life Cycle Assessment from a coupled energy-carbon-water (ECW) nexus perspective; key LCA concepts; the LCA process; LCA standards; application of LCA approaches and software to assess the energy, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, water, and other environmental impacts of building construction industry at the material and whole building levels; study and analysis of factors relating to material and assembly choices, site logistics, on-site and off-site construction and/or fabrication processes, additive construction (large-scale 3D printing), and construction and demolition waste to reduce the energy use, GHG emissions, and water use; analysis and comparison of LCA results of process-based and macro-economic model-based Life Cycle Inventory (LCI). Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: COSC
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Life Cycle Assessment in Building Construction. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to Life Cycle Assessment from a coupled energy-carbon-water (ECW) nexus perspective; Key LCA concepts; the LCA process; LCA standards; application of LCA approaches and software to assess the energy, greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions, water, and other environmental impacts of building construction industry at the material and whole building levels; study and analysis of factors relating to material and assembly choices, site logistics, on-site and off­ site construction and/or fabrication processes, additive construction (large-scale 3D printing), and construction and demolition waste to reduce the energy use, GHG emissions, and water use; analysis and comparison of LCA results of process-based and macro-economic model-based Life Cycle Inventory (LCI). Prerequisite: Graduate classification in the Department of Construction Science.

Law and policy issues related to cybersecurity including procurement, operations, maintenance, governance, oversight, protection, defense; analyze law, policies, and regulations domestically and globally. subject: CSCE
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Cybersecurity Risk. (3-0). Credit 3. Risks in cybersecurity; avoidance, acceptance, mitigation or transference strategies; developing reliable cybersecurity risk assessments to include analysis, categorization and evaluation; cybersecurity risk audit frameworks. Prerequisites: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with CYBR 603.

subject: CSCE
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Data Analytics for Cybersecurity. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the theoretical foundations, algorithms and methods of data analytics for cybersecurity; societally-critical topic with impacts across computing systems and networks, social and web-based communities, industrial control systems and personal devices, among many others; study and application of data analytics including cluster analysis, supervised machine learning, anomaly detection and visualization; addresses a suite of cybersecurity topics including cyber attacks, anomaly detection, vulnerability analysis, strategic manipulation and propaganda. Prerequisites: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with CYBR 604.

prerequisite_text: Graduate classification in civil engineering or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_text: CVEN 615, CVEN 616 or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_text: CVEN 444 or equivalent.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Advanced Reinforced Concrete Design. (3-0). Credit 3. Reinforced concrete principles; analysis of rigid building frames, design of building frames, slabs, biaxially loaded columns, rectangular and circular tanks, and deep beams. Prerequisite: CVEN 444 or equivalent.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification in Civil Engineering, Aerospace Engineering or Mechanical Engineering.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: System Identification and Nondestructive Damage Evaluation of Civil Engineering Structures. (3-0). Credit 3. Inevasive assessment of civil structures; concepts of systems identification, damage detection, and safety evaluation; estimation of mass, damping, and stiffness properties; determination of load capacity and useful life. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in Civil Engineering, Aerospace Engineering or Mechanical Engineering.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: CVEN 672 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Transportation Engineering: Economics. (3-0). Credit 3. Engineering and economic principles for transportation systems; engineering evaluation using methods of travel demand, costs, equilibrium and pricing; use of economic principles for the finance, engineering and management of transportation systems. Prerequisite: CVEN 672 or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: CVEN 405 and CVEN 473 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Methods Improvement for Construction Engineers. (3-0). Credit 3. Application of work methods and measurements to civil engineering construction; examination of factors that affect productivity in construction; study of motivational factors; review of the principles of accident prevention. Prerequisites: CVEN 405 and CVEN 473 or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: Strong analytical background; approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Water-Energy-Food Nexus: Toward Sustainable Resource Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Principles and application of the Water-Energy-Food nexus to state, national and international Water-Energy-Food securities and the interlinkages between them; exploration of quantitative framework to develop and assess sustainable tradeoffs of resources; hands on experiences; relevant real world projects or case studies. Prerequisites: Strong analytical background; approval of instructor. Cross-listed with BAEN 642.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: (s): STAT 601 or equivalent; graduate status in Engineering, approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Project Risk Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Identifies causes of risks in projects; discusses probabilistic description of risks and formulation of risk models; Bayesian methods for revising probabilities; qualitative and quantitative risk assessment; setting contingencies on budgets and schedules; risk mitigation and risk management; handling technological risk; Utility theory and game theory in management of risks. Prerequisites: (s): STAT 601 or equivalent; graduate status in Engineering, approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: MATH 308.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Soil Dynamics. (3-0). Credit 3. Dynamic properties of soil; wave propagation in an elastic medium; analysis of dynamic soil-structure interaction and machine foundations; earthquake engineering; soil liquefaction; seismic design of foundations, dams, retaining walls and pipelines. Prerequisite: MATH 308.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Civil Engineering Applications of GIS. (2-2). Credit 3. Use of geographic information system (GIS) concepts and methods to solve civil engineering problems; emphasis on different areas of civil engineering. Class presentations and laboratory sessions used to familiarize students with computer software. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: 3 credit hours of structural steel design or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Behavior and Design of Steel Structures. (3-0). Credit 3. Buckling and post-buckling strength of stiffened and unstiffened plate elements and members; torsional behavior and design of beams; stability of frames; frames subject to sidesway; bracing design; non-destructive evaluation and application of fracture mechanics principles to welded structures. Prerequisite: 3 credit hours of structural steel design or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification in engineering.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Experimental Methods in Civil Engineering. (2-3). Credit 3. Introduction to experimental methods, instrumentation, data acquisition and data processing; experimental aspects of static and dynamic testing in the various areas of civil engineering; overview of laboratory work with several hands-on applications in the laboratory. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in engineering.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification in engineering or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Water Resources Engineering Planning and Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Managing water resources; the planning process, systems analysis methods; institutional framework for water resources engineering; comprehensive integration of engineering, economic, environmental, legal and political considerations in water resources development and management. Prerequisite: Graduate classification in engineering or approval of instructor.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: CVEN 339; CVEN 422 or equivalent.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Water Resources Systems Engineering. (3-0). Credit 3. Linear and non-linear optimization models and simulation models for planning and management of water systems; single- and multi-objective analysis and deterministic and stochastic techniques. Prerequisites: CVEN 339; CVEN 422 or equivalent.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Foundation Structures. (2-3). Credit 3. Geological and soil mechanics principles including load bearing capacity, soil pressure and settlement; design of shallow foundation sub-structures including pedestals, spread footings, combined footings, mats and underream footings; design of deep foundations including piles and drilled piers; retaining walls, cofferdams and sheet piles.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_text: CVEN 365 or equivalent; graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Slope Stability and Retaining Walls. (2-2). Credit 3. Slope stability; failure analysis including methods of slices; risk analysis; earthquake analysis; monitoring; remedial measures; retaining structures; basic theories; gravity walls; cantilever walls; tieback walls; mechanically stabilized walls; soil nailing; deflecting-based analysis. Prerequisites: CVEN 365 or equivalent; graduate classification.

subject: CVEN
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Civil Engineering Project Finance. (3-0). Credit 3. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

Prerequisite: CVEN 444, CVEN 445, and CVEN 446; graduate classification in civil engineering or approval of instructor.

subject: ECDE
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Partnering with Families in Early Childhood. (3-0). Credit 3. Application of an ecological model to the understanding of variation in family roles, perspectives, approaches, strengths, and goals; effective communication and partnership approaches for families of young children; family education programming. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification.

subject: ECDE
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in EDCI 353 or concurrent enrollment.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Early Childhood Math, Science, and Play. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of mathematics and science through play and exploration; number sense, counting, place value, early geometry, and algebraic thinking; scientific practices such as inquiry, observation, experimentation, patterns, cause and effect, and systems. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in EDCI 353 or concurrent enrollment.

subject: ECEN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in PHYS 207; grade of C or better in PHYS 217 or ENGR 217; grade of C or better in CHEM 107, CHEM 102, or CHEM 120; grade of C or better in MATH 308, or concurrent enrollment.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Electrical Circuit Theory. (3-3). Credit 4. Resistive circuits including circuit laws, network reduction, nodal analysis, mesh analysis; introduction to operational amplifiers; circuit analysis with inductors and capacitors; sinusoidal steady state circuit analysis; AC power calculations; magnetically coupled circuits; the ideal transformer; resonance; introduction to circuit simulation. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHYS 207; grade of C or better in PHYS 217 or ENGR 217; grade of C or better in CHEM 107, CHEM 102, or CHEM 120; grade of C or better in MATH 308, or concurrent enrollment.

subject: ECEN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ultrasound Imaging. (3-0). Credit 3. Mathematical analysis of wave propagation, scattering of ultrasound in biological tissues, electronic transducer arrays for the beam forming, models of the received signals and signal processing methods for medical ultrasound imaging of tissues; includes discussions of research related to fundamental ultrasound imaging concepts. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 340, and ECEN 420 or ECEN 460; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Physical and Economical Operations of Sustainable Energy Systems. (3-0). Credit 3. Operational issues for sustainable electric energy systems; basic relevant topics in engineering, optimization and economic concepts; modular view of individual electric energy processing components; physical and market operations in electricity industry in support of sustainable energy integration; computer simulations and demonstrations to create and evaluate examples of power systems. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 340, and ECEN 420 or ECEN 460; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314 and MATH 308; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Linear Control Systems. (3-0). Credit 3. Application of state variable and frequency domain techniques to modeling, analysis and synthesis of single input, single output linear control systems. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314 and MATH 308; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 311; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Computer and Wireless Networks. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamentals of wired and wireless computer networks, design and performance evaluations of wired and wireless networks, various unguided media characterizations and classifications/comparisons, digital-data representations/transmissions, error control, MAC protocols, routing, TCP/UDP/IP, wireless TCP, queuing-delay/loss modeling, IEEE 802.11 and its interconnections with Internet, and QoS provisioning over wired/wireless networks. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in MATH 311; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Radio Frequency and Microwave Engineering. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamental Radio Frequency (RF) and microwave circuit analysis including scattering and ABCD matrices, return loss, insertion loss; transmission lines, lumped elements, impedance matching; theory, analysis and design of basic RF and microwave passive circuits; use of commercial CAD programs for RF and microwave circuit design and simulation. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 322; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 304, MATH 311, or MATH 323; Grade of C or better in STAT 211, and STAT 404 or CSCE 221, or ECEN 303, and CSCE 121 or CSCE 120.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Machine Learning. (3-0). Credit 3. Theoretical foundations of machine learning, pattern recognition and generating predictive models and classifiers from data; includes methods for supervised and unsupervised learning (decision trees, linear discriminants, neural networks, Gaussian models, non-parametric models, clustering, dimensionality reduction, deep learning), optimization procedures and statistical inference. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 304, MATH 311, or MATH 323; Grade of C or better in STAT 211, and STAT 404 or CSCE 221, or ECEN 303, and CSCE 121 or CSCE 120. Cross-listed with CSCE 421 and STAT 421.

subject: ECEN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314 and ECEN 325; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Data Conversion Systems and Circuits. (3-3). Credit 4. Sampling theory and sampling circuit implementations, quantization architectures and interpolation techniques for data conversion interfaces such as analog-to-digital and digital-to-analog converters, noise modeling of sampled and quantized data, performance metrics, modeling of circuits errors (capacitor mismatch, gain mismatches, etc.) basic linear calibration techniques and compensation techniques. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314 and ECEN 325; junior or senior classification.

subject: ECEN
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314 and ECEN 325; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Audio Engineering. (3-0). Credits 3. Sound propagation, psychoacoustics, electroacoustics and architectural acoustics for the design and application of audio technology. Auditory system and audio perception concepts such as pitch, loudness, timbre, masking, apparent location. Speakers, microphones, and other electroacoustic transducers, enclosures and the mixers and the audio power amplifiers used to drive them. Architectural and environmental acoustics building acoustics, reflecting and absorbent materials, noise barriers, echoes, presence, reverberation, resonance. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in ECEN 314 and ECEN 325; junior or senior classification.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Topics in the History of the English Language. (3-0). Credit 3. Topics in the development of the English language; may include phonological, grammatical and lexical histories; study of social and political contexts; relationships between English and other languages. May be taken three times for credit as content varies. Cross-listed with LING 610.

subject: ENGL
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Readings in Eighteenth-Century British Literature. (3-0). Credit 3. Wide reading in British literature of the 18th Century; introduction of major figures, genres, and issues in the period; introduction to current critical conversations in 18th Century literary studies, including historical and social contexts.

subject: ENGL
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Topics in 18th and 19th Century British Literature and Culture. (3-0). Credit 3. Topics in the history, theory, interpretation of 18th and/or 19th Century British literature and culture; may focus on authors, groups of authors, themes, movements, genres, cultural contexts and/or theoretical framing. May be taken three times for credit as content varies.

subject: ENGL
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Readings in 20th and 21st Century Literature and Culture. (3-0). Credit 3. Wide reading in 20th and 21st Century literature; introduction of major figures, genres, and issues in the period; introduction to current critical conversations in modern and postmodern literary studies, including historical and social contexts.

subject: ENGL
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Topics in 20th and 21st Century Literature and Culture. (3-0). Credit 3. prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Research in Writing Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. Methods, practice, and theory in writing studies; readings in scholarship on writing and its subgenres, such as technical, scientific, grant, business, global, health, or digital writing; introduction to methods for writing studies research; examination of the practice of writing in given genres for particular audiences. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

subject: ENGL
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Topics in Cultural/Interdisciplinary Studies. (3-0). Credit 3. May be taken three times for credit as content varies.

subject: ENGL
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Topics in Textual Studies and Book History. (3-0). Credit 3. Topics in the theory and practice of textual studies and book history; may focus on the book as material object, histories of printing and other technologies, digital humanities, book production and distribution, research methodologies. May be taken three times for credit as content varies.

May be taken three times for credit as content varies.

prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 151 or MATH 171 or equivalent; grade of C or better in ENGR 102; grade of C or better in PHYS 206 or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Experimental Physics and Engineering Lab II - Mechanics. (1-3). Credit 2. Description and application of laws of physical motion to the solution of science and engineering problems; using sensing, control and actuation for experimental verification of physics concepts while solving engineering problems. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in MATH 151 or MATH 171 or equivalent; grade of C or better in ENGR 102; grade of C or better in PHYS 206 or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus. Cross-listed with PHYS 216.

prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 151 or MATH 171 or equivalent; grade of C or better in ENGR 102; grade of C or better in PHYS 206 or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Experimental Physics and Engineering Lab II - Mechanics. (1-3). Credit 2. Cross-listed with PHYS 216.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Biomedical Genetics. (3-0). Credit 3. Study of modern genetics with an emphasis on biomedical and health-related applications of the mammalian genome. Topics include classical Mendelian inheritance, pedigree and genetic risk analysis, population genetics, quantitative genetics and the molecular basis of gene structure and function, including DNA replication, transcription, mutation and gene regulation. The course examines how genetic variation and chromosomal abnormalities contribute to disease and phenotypic diversity, and introduces advanced concepts in cytogenetics, epigenetics, cancer genetics and genomics. Contemporary applications such as genome sequencing, gene therapy, personalized medicine and associated ethical considerations are also addressed. Only one of the following will satisfy the requirements for a degree: GENE 301, GENE 302, GENE 315, GENE-320 or BIMS-320. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 228 or CHEM 258; PHYS 207 or grade of C or better in PHYS 202; junior or senior classification. Cross-listed with BIMS 320.

subject: GENE
prerequisite_text: ENTO 601 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Quantitative Phylogenetics. (3-4). Credit 4. Designed to provide the theory and tools required for inference of phylogenetic (evolutionary) relationships among biological taxa using various types of comparative data including morphological characters, biochemical and molecular characters, and DNA sequences; hands-on analysis of data using contemporary tools. Prerequisite: ENTO 601 or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ENTO 606 and ECCB 606.

subject: GENE
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification in biochemistry, biochemistry and molecular biophysics, genetics, genetics and genomics, or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Mechanisms of Cell Division. (1-0). Credit 1. Mitotic cell cycle; progression of biochemical and morphological phases and events; duplication of cellular constituents and segregation into daughter cells. Prerequisites: Graduate classification in biochemistry, biochemistry and molecular biophysics, genetics, genetics and genomics, or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with BICH 616.

subject: GENE
prerequisite_text: GENE 603.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Cytogenetics. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination and analysis of variation in chromosome structure, behavior and number; developmental and evolutionary effects of this variation. Prerequisite: GENE 603.

subject: GENE
prerequisite_text: GENE 603 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Applied Animal Genomics. (3-0). Credit 3. Theory and application of genomics by livestock industries; consideration of genetic markers, gene mapping methods, genome analysis and emerging technologies such as microarrays, transgenesis, cloning and marker assisted selection; exposure to bioinformatic tools for genomics. Prerequisite: GENE 603 or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ANSC 629 and POSC 630.

subject: GENE
prerequisite_text: GENE 603 or GENE 431.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Analysis of Complex Genomes. (3-0). Credit 3. History and current status of genetic and molecular analysis of higher eukaryotic genomes; coverage of techniques for dissection of genomes into manageable parts; investigations in genetics, breeding and evolution; emphasis on quantitative inheritance, genetic mapping, physical mapping, map-based cloning, with examples drawn from a wide range of organisms. Prerequisite: GENE 603 or GENE 431. Cross-listed with SCSC 654 and MEPS 654.

subject: GENE
prerequisite_text: GENE 603 or equivalent or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Analysis of Complex Genomes--Lab. (0-7). Credit 3. Laboratory methods in molecular genetic techniques for genetic mapping, physical mapping, and map-based cloning of both qualitative and quantitative phenotypes. Prerequisite: GENE 603 or equivalent or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with SCSC 655 and MEPS 655.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Environmental Justice. (3-0). Credit 3. This course examines the uneven distribution of environmental benefits and burdens across society, drawing on the scholarly literature referred to as environmental justice research. You will examine historical and contemporary evidence for disparities in exposure to environmental hazards, including but not limited to air and water pollution, as well as disparities in access to environmental amenities, including but not limited to urban greenspace. Topics address variation in environmental conditions and policy outcomes across different demographic and geographic contexts, including those associated with race, gender, ethnicity and class, as these social categories are used in empirical research and policy analysis. The course treats these social categories as analytical descriptors rather than normative or ideological claims. Content includes controversial and contested scholarly perspectives on environmental issues, reflecting multiple explanatory frameworks for understanding the causes of and proposed policy responses to uneven environmental distributions. Drawing on readings from a range of disciplines, such as environmental science, geography and urban planning, you will evaluate proposed explanations for observed patterns, including but not limited to market dynamics, land-use decisions, regulatory enforcement, historical settlement patterns and institutional decision-making processes. You will also compare policy and governance responses discussed in the scholarly literature, such as market-based mechanisms, participatory decision-making arrangements and strengthened regulatory oversight, assessing their assumptions, empirical support and trade-offs. The course emphasizes evidence-based reasoning and civil discourse, preparing you to engage constructively with contentious environmental policy contexts. An independent research project will train you to develop and defend an analytical argument related to an environmental justice issue of your choosing using appropriate evidence. Throughout the course, your work will be evaluated on the quality of analysis and reasoning, not on agreement with any particular political, moral or ideological position. Prerequisites: GEOG 201 or GEOG 202; junior or senior classification.

subject: GEOL
prerequisite_text: CHEM 119 or equivalent; GEOL 152 or equivalent.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Sedimentology and Stratigraphy. (3-3). Credit 4. Origin of sediments and sedimentary rocks; climate, weathering, and weathering products; transport, deposition, and depositional environments for sediments; field and laboratory studies in description and interpretation of genesis of sedimentary rocks; principles of stratigraphy and basin analysis; plate tectonics and the formation of sedimentary basins; stratigraphic nomenclature; geologic time and correlation; sequence stratigraphy and basin architecture. Prerequisite: CHEM 119 or equivalent; GEOL 152 or equivalent.

subject: GEOL
prerequisite_text: GEOL 101 and GEOL 102, or GEOL 104, or GEOL 150.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Planetary Geology. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to planetary science; organization and composition of the solar system, including the planets, satellites and asteroids; surface features and internal structures of the terrestrial planets and moons; the dynamic processes of planetary resurfacing, including volcanism, tectonism, weathering and impacts; the history and future of solar system exploration. Prerequisites: GEOL 101 and GEOL 102, or GEOL 104, or GEOL 150.

subject: GEOL
prerequisite_text: GEOL 101 and GEOL 102, or GEOL 104, or GEOL 150; MATH 142 or MATH 152; PHYS 201 or PHYS 206.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Structural Geology and Tectonics. (3-3). Credit 4. Fundamentals of the deformation of the lithosphere ranging from plate to atomic scales; stress, strain, experimental rock deformation, microscopic mechanisms and mechanical behaviors; analysis of faults, folds, flow and rock fabrics; subsurface interpretation; regional tectonics of selected areas; practical experience in geometric and kinematic analysis, constructing balanced cross sections. Prerequisites: GEOL 101 and GEOL 102, or GEOL 104, or GEOL 150; MATH 142 or MATH 152; PHYS 201 or PHYS 206.
