subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: PBSI 107.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Psychology of Culture and Diversity. (3-0). Credit 3. Explore how culture shapes psychological processes and how psychology explains cultural variation. Analyze cultural influences on cognition, emotion, motivation, identity and mental health. Examine the development and scientific study of culture and discuss how cultural contact and acculturation affect adaptation and intergroup relations. Apply psychological frameworks to understand global diversity and the dynamic relationship between individuals and their cultural environments. Prerequisites: PBSI 107. Cross-listed with AFST 209.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: PBSI 107.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Psychological Aspects of Human Sexuality. (3-0). Credit 3. Examine human sexuality through biological, psychological, social, relational and cultural lenses. Analyze reproductive anatomy, gender roles, sexual identity, sexual orientation and sexual behavior across the lifespan. Explore topics including love, attraction, sexual health, sexual victimization, diversity and sexuality as a commodity. Apply the bio-psycho-social-cultural model to understand how various factors shape sexual experiences and attitudes. Develop skills to assess sexual health, promote well-being and articulate what healthy sexuality means. Prerequisite: PBSI 107. Cross-listed with WGST 210.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (PSYC 2314) Lifespan Development. (3-0). Credit 3. Explore human psychological development from conception through late adulthood, focusing on how individuals grow, change and adapt across life stages. Examine major theoretical perspectives and empirical research on emotional, cognitive, personality and social development. Investigate biological influences, cultural factors and social relationships that shape behavior and identity over time. Analyze key transitions such as infancy, adolescence, emerging adulthood and aging through evidence-based inquiry. Strengthen critical thinking and problem-solving skills while interpreting developmental claims using scientific methods. Gain insight into the dynamic interplay of nature and nurture and apply psychological principles to personal, professional and societal contexts.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: PBSI 107 or BIOL 111.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Introduction to Behavioral and Cognitive Neuroscience. (3-0). Credit 3. Investigate the biological foundations of human thought, emotion and behavior through an introduction to cellular, behavioral and cognitive neuroscience. Examine how psychological processes emerge from neural structures and functions, integrating insights from cellular mechanisms to complex cognitive phenomena. Topics include neural anatomy and physiology, sensory and motor systems, sleep and circadian rhythms, emotion and stress, learning and memory, attention, language and mental disorders. Analyze current research and foundational theories using evidence from both human neuroscience techniques and animal models. Build a strong conceptual framework for understanding how brain activity supports cognition and behavior, preparing for advanced study in neuroscience, psychology and related disciplines. Prerequisites: PBSI 107 or BIOL 111.

Investigate major theories and research on topics such as social perception, attitudes and persuasion, conformity, group dynamics, prejudice, cultural influences, self and identity, aggression, prosocial behavior and interpersonal relationships. Analyze the power of social situations and group processes in shaping individual behavior. Apply psychological frameworks to interpret personal experiences, social interactions and broader societal patterns. Evaluate empirical findings and consider diverse perspectives to gain insight into the complexity of human behavior in social contexts. Strengthen critical thinking while developing a deeper understanding of how individuals influence and are influenced by others. Prerequisite: PBSI 107.

Critically evaluate research and practice to understand how psychological principles guide effective decision-making in personnel management. Prerequisites: PBSI 107; PBSI 245, MATH 140, MATH 168, MATH 142, MATH 147, MATH 151, MATH 171, MATH 152, MATH 148, MATH 172, MATH 150, PHIL 240 or STAT 201; PBSI 301 and PBSI 302 recommended.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification; grade of C or better in PBSI 107.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Qualitative Methods in the Psychological Sciences. (3-0). Credit 3. Research methods and approaches to engaging in qualitative analysis; topics include epistemological and ontological assumptions of qualitative research, ethical considerations, focus groups, interviews, qualitative surveys, thematic analysis, and use of qualitative software. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; grade of C or better in PBSI 107.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: PBSI 107.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Existential Psychology . (3-0). Credit 3. Study of major theoretical perspectives and contemporary research in existential psychology; focus on theory and research examining major topics in existential psychology including the causes and consequences of mortality awareness, self-knowledge, authenticity, belief in free-will and the experience of meaning in life. Prerequisite: PBSI 107.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: PBSI 107.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Psychology of Emotion. (3-0). Credit 3. Examination of the theories and approaches in the psychological study of emotion; topics related to emotion, including predictors of happiness, causes and consequences of emotion, and the role of emotion in society; identification of facial expressions of emotion; examination of techniques that promote happiness. Prerequisites: PBSI 107.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Psychological and Social Determinants of Health Disparities. (3-0). Credit 3. Examine psychological, social, cultural and societal contributors to health disparities in the United States. Analyze how macrosocial factors — such as socioeconomic status, discrimination, gender, religion and geography — affect physical and mental health through mechanisms like stress, healthcare access and cultural inputs. Explore historical and contemporary patterns of morbidity and mortality using interdisciplinary research from psychology, sociology, public health and behavioral science. Strengthen critical thinking and scientific writing while evaluating conceptual models and empirical evidence. Topics and focal groups will vary by instructor. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ethics and Techniques in Clinical Psychology. (3-0). Credit 3. Develop foundational competencies for ethical and effective clinical practice as a scientist-practitioner. Engage with ethical decision-making in clinical practice and research contexts, learn foundational clinical interviewing and diagnostic techniques and apply skills for building and maintaining the therapeutic alliance in cognitive-behavioral therapy. Emphasize the integration of scientific evidence with clinical application to support accurate diagnosis and ethical treatment. Learning outcomes are aligned with the American Psychological Association Profession-Wide Competencies to prepare for professional roles in clinical psychology. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Theories of Social Psychology. (3-0). Credit 3. Examine the major theoretical frameworks that shape contemporary social psychology. Analyze how classic and emerging theories explain social behavior, cognition and emotion. Evaluate the historical development, empirical support and practical implications of key theories. Engage critically with theoretical debates and apply conceptual models to real-world social phenomena. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Seminar in Social Psychology. Credit 3. Engage deeply with advanced and emerging topics in social psychology through a thematic seminar that varies each semester. Explore topics such as attitudes and persuasion; self-regulation; motivation; self and identity; applied social problems; moral psychology; existential social psychology; emotion; social cognition; stereotypes and prejudice. Critically analyze primary literature to uncover theoretical and empirical insights, identify gaps in current research and generate innovative questions. Integrate diverse perspectives to develop a nuanced understanding of complex social phenomena and refine ideas for future research. May be taken five times for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Enrollment in Clinical Psychology Graduate Program or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Clinical Psychology Interventions I. (3-0). Credit 3. Explore foundational theory, research and techniques for delivering evidence-based psychological interventions. Focus on cognitive-behavioral and related approaches to treating various forms of psychopathology. Examine classical and contemporary models to build depth in understanding therapeutic strategies. Engage with ethical, professional and historical perspectives that shape clinical practice. Prerequisite: Enrollment in Clinical Psychology Graduate Program or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: PBSI 685, EPSY 685, PBSI 691, or EPSY 691, or approval of instructor; graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Pediatric Psychology. (3-0). Credit 3. Application of clinical/counseling/school psychology to children and adolescents with chronic illnesses or disabilities and their families; theoretical foundations and models for consultation, assessment and intervention strategies; unique ethical and professional issues associated with research and service delivery in child health psychology/pediatric behavioral medicine. Prerequisite: PBSI 685, EPSY 685, PBSI 691, or EPSY 691, or approval of instructor; graduate classification.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Seminar in Cognition and Cognitive Neuroscience. Credit 3. Survey of research in cognition and cognitive neuroscience; attention; memory; decision making; language; bilingualism; creativity; cognitive control; motor control; aging; learning; adjustment; perception; psychophysics. May be taken four times for credit as content varies. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
course_title: ADV DATA ANLY I/O PSYC PROF II
prerequisite_text: PBSI 652; graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Advanced Data Analytics for Industrial/Organizational Psychology Professionals II. (3-0). Credit 3. Advance analytical expertise in industrial-organizational psychology through hands-on application of complex statistical techniques. Explore methods such as exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling and logistic regression to uncover insights from workplace data. Discuss the design and implementation of organizational surveys, evaluating item quality and data integrity. Strengthen the ability to integrate conceptual knowledge with practical software tools to support evidence-based decision making in professional settings. Prerequisites: PBSI 652; graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Foundations in Cognitive Neuroscience. (3-0). Credit 3. Experimental design in cognitive neuroscience; basics of cognitive neuroscience methods; perception versus imagery; attention; motor control; short-term and long-term memory; volition and consciousness; executive function; decision making; affect and psychopathology; social cognition. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with NRSC 655.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Training and Performance Management. (3-0). Credit 3. Examine the psychological foundations and evidence-based practices of training and performance management to enhance individual, team and organizational effectiveness. Explore contemporary theories and methods in learning and development, including instructional systems design, adult learning theory and AI-enabled training. Analyze tools such as electronic performance monitoring, learning management systems and 360-degree feedback. Investigate strategies for identifying high-potential employees and aligning performance interventions with organizational goals. Emphasize inclusive approaches that account for adult learners’ experiences and demographics, integrating research from industrial-organizational psychology to inform practical applications. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Work Attitudes and Motivation. (3-0). Credit 3. This course explores the psychological factors that shape employee attitudes, motivation and withdrawal behaviors like absenteeism and turnover. It covers key concepts — job satisfaction, organizational commitment, engagement, stress and work values — and how they affect both employees and organizations. Students examine common tools for measuring workplace attitudes and motivation and learn to use insights from social and organizational psychology to diagnose workplace issues and recommend evidence-based solutions. The course emphasizes connecting theory with practical application to build strong analytical and applied skills for diverse organizational settings. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Methods and Statistics in Psychological Science II. (2-3). Credit 3. Examine the conceptual foundations and practical applications of linear regression in psychological research. Focus on understanding the rationale behind regression-based approaches and develop proficiency in selecting, applying and interpreting appropriate models for behavioral data. Gain hands-on experience with psychological datasets and enhance analytical thinking through guided practice. Emphasize the integration of statistical reasoning with empirical inquiry to support sound research conclusions. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with NRSC 671.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Qualitative Methods in Psychological Sciences. (3-0). Credit 3. Overview of psychology qualitative methods; assumptions of qualitative research; focus groups; qualitative analysis software; thematic analysis. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: PBSI 607 and PBSI 671 or equivalents.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Psychometric Theory and Methods. Credit 3. Overview of methods for the construction and evaluation of psychological measurements including unidimensional scales and multi-variate analytical techniques; approaches include classical test theory, factor analysis, unidimensional scaling, latent trait theory, profile and discriminant analysis. Prerequisites: PBSI 607 and PBSI 671 or equivalents.

subject: PBSI
prerequisite_text: PBSI 610 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Seminar in Organizational Psychology. Credit 3. Engage with advanced theoretical and empirical literature in organizational psychology to critically evaluate key constructs and research methodologies. Compare and contrast major theories, assess scientific findings and identify future research directions. Emphasis is placed on developing analytical skills through the examination of research design, data interpretation and methodological rigor across varied organizational contexts. Topics will vary across instructors and have included but are not limited to job stress, occupational health, diversity in organizations, job attitudes, motivation, organizational behavior and leadership. May be taken six times for credit. Prerequisite: PBSI 610 or approval of instructor.

subject: PHEO
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Chemical Hazard Exposure. (3-0). Credit 3. Methods for sampling hazardous chemicals in various environmental media; planning the sample collection; analytical process to ensure that data quality is sufficient to meet project objectives; Data Quality Objectives; development of a QAPP and QA/QC protocols including data validation. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

subject: PHEO
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Global Environmental Health. (3-0). Credit 3. Review of the globalization and transformation of local problems into international issues; environmental problems that developing and underdeveloped countries face due to overpopulation, lack of natural resources and lack of proper ways or technologies to dispose of hazardous wastes. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

subject: PHEO
prerequisite_text: College-level mathematics.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Environmental/Occupational Diseases. (3-0). Credit 3. Identification, evaluation and quantification of risk factors for environmental and occupational diseases, using classic and current examples of exposures involving chemical, physical and biologic agents; selection of appropriate design and groups; exposure assessment, including biomarkers and molecular dosimetry; genetics, gender, age, socioeconomic and other factors affecting susceptibility. May be taken two times for credit. Prerequisite: College-level mathematics.

subject: PHEO
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Hazardous Materials Management and Compliance. (3-0). Credit 3. Types of hazardous materials; system of environmental laws governing management of hazardous materials as well as contaminants in air, water and solid waste; appropriate management and regulatory compliance; hazardous materials spills and response; hazard communication and right-to-know regulations; hazard communication benchmarking and performance criteria. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

subject: PHEO
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Hazardous Materials Management and Compliance. (3-0). Credit 3. subject: PHEO
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Industrial Hygiene. (3-0). Credit 3. Considers methods to measure and reduce workplace hazards; evaluation of engineering controls and personal protective equipment; includes potential chemical, physical, ergonomic and biological exposures. Review of major legislation affecting workplace environment. Prerequisites: Graduate classification.

subject: PHEO
course_title: HLTH  SAFETY AT HAZ WST SITES
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Health and Safety at Hazardous Waste Sites. (3-0). Credit 3. Course covers OSHA compliance issues related to the protection of personnel engaged in on-site remediation activities. Students who satisfactorily complete the course meet the requirements for initial training under 20 CFR 1910.120 (HAZWOPER) and receive a certificate. Hands-on activities/workshops in the areas of personal protective equipment selection and use, sources of chemical information, decontamination procedures, air monitoring equipment, materials handling, and health and safety planning. Lab fee required.

subject: PHEO
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Human Factors. (3-0). Credit 3. Basic understanding of the theory and practice of human factors as well as application of these to an industry project; topics presented within the framework of humans being part of a functioning systems.

subject: PHEO
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ergonomics of the Upper Extremities. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamental topics upon which models for the prevention and control of distal upper extremity disorders are constructed. Focus is on topics including human anatomy, neurophysiology, electrophysiology and worker capacity evaluation.

subject: PHEO
prerequisite_text: Approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Industrial and System Safety. (3-0). Credit 3. Course covers general concepts and techniques of safety upon which more detailed and advanced applications may be based. In addition, concepts will include current system safety analysis techniques, failure mode and effect and fault tree analysis, as well as economic analysis for presentation of alternative solutions for problem solving. Prerequisite: Approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
attributes_json: ["College Station", "Core Lang, Phil, Culture(KLPC)", "Univ Req-Cult Discourse (KUCD)"]
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: (PHIL 2306) Contemporary Moral Issues. (3-0). Credit 3. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students evaluate the claims, presuppositions and reasoning of various positions, including one’s own, on contemporary social problems and analyze those problems using ethical and social theories. Students examine how ideas, values and other aspects of culture (including power and authority) shape and are shaped by human experience and institutions. Students practice respectful and thoughtful engagement on contentious matters, such as abortion, euthanasia, capital punishment, the relationship between ethics and religion, violence and war, animal ethics, sexual morality, gender issues, health care ethics, equality and discrimination, biotechnology and bioengineering, economic injustice, climate ethics and global hunger and poverty, among others; also taught at Galveston campus.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ethics in a Digital Age. (3-0). Credit 3. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students practice respectful, thoughtful and self-aware engagement to prepare them to navigate a variety of cultural environments; also taught at Galveston campus.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Social and Political Philosophy. (3-0). Credit 3. Philosophy challenge students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students investigate key questions, concepts and debates in social and political thought, including those that were particularly influential on the founding generation of the United States. Sources include canonical primary texts but may also encompass more contemporary or critical responses to the canon. Emphasis is on fundamental problems in political life and may include: the source of political authority, the just distribution of the burdens and benefits of social life, the limits of state authority, the essence of political community, citizenship or responsibilities of civic life. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Philosophy of Law. (3-0). Credit 3. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students survey debates regarding foundational philosophical issues about the law. While the specific issues covered may vary from semester to semester, paradigmatic topics include: what makes a law a law, the relation of law to morality, the appropriate aim of criminal punishment, the basis of criminal responsibility, methods for interpreting the U.S. Constitution, the scope or limits of a specific constitutional right, the obligation to obey the law and civil disobedience, critiques of liberalism and the aim of tort law. Students examine major jurisprudential theories — such as natural law, positivism, realism and critical and phenomenological approaches — to understand how legal systems define justice, obligation and authority. Readings include both historical and contemporary jurisprudence as well as case law. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PHIL
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Advanced Topics in Philosophy of Law. (3-0). Credit 3. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students pursue focused and in-depth study of a specific topic in philosophy of law. The topic changes semester to semester. Recent versions focused on: the meaning and scope of First Amendment rights, the legal protection of privacy, the history of differing conceptions of the rule of law, modern theories of legal positivism and realism and the study of legal ontology, which investigates the ways in which laws and legal institutions exist relative to other social objects. Readings are drawn from historical and/or contemporary jurisprudence as well as case law. Students design and execute independent research projects connected to the theme of the seminar. Contact the department for information about the theme for an upcoming semester. May be taken three times for credit. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor.

Students may read works by philosophers in addition to novelists and essayists.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ethics and Engineering. (2-2). Credit 3. Philosophy challenges students to understand, articulate and evaluate arguments from multiple points of view. Students explore ethical and social theories, principles and engineering codes of ethics and their application to ethical challenges faced by engineers. Students engage with issues, such as satisfying responsibilities to an employer, client, fellow employees, one’s profession and the public; managing project pressures, risks, liability, regulations and environmental concerns. Students practice resolving challenges that arise from varying norms found in international and cross-cultural initiatives, especially on gifts, bribes and extortion. Students critically consider the ways engineers and engineering change the human experience, cultures and the environment. Students practice respectful and thoughtful dialogue on contemporary issues, become aware of their own perspectives and understand how power and authority are exercised in and shape institutions so that they can competently navigate a variety of cultural environments. Coursework focuses on independent ethical analysis of real and hypothetical cases and on the techniques that can be used to evaluate them. Prerequisite: Junior classification.

Students explore ethical and social theories, principles and engineering codes of ethics and their application to ethical challenges faced by engineers. Students engage with issues, such as satisfying responsibilities to an employer, client, fellow employees, one’s profession and the public; managing project pressures, risks, liability, regulations and environmental concerns. Students practice resolving challenges that arise from varying norms found in international and cross-cultural initiatives, especially on gifts, bribes and extortion. Students critically consider the ways engineers and engineering change the human experience, cultures and the environment. Students practice respectful and thoughtful dialogue on contemporary issues, become aware of their own perspectives and understand how power and authority are exercised in and shape institutions so that they can competently navigate a variety of cultural environments. Coursework focuses on independent ethical analysis of real and hypothetical cases and on the techniques that can be used to evaluate them. Prerequisite: Junior classification.

subject: PHPM
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Global Health. (3-0). Credit 3. Globalization of health is evolving dramatically spurred on by the globalization of trade and commerce, migration of peoples, and advances in communication. These changes are having a significant impact on health and health care. Multiple diseases, as influenza, emerging in a local site but then are transmitted at a global or pandemic proportion with a few short weeks or months. International travel and the migration of populations across countries can lead to the introduction of diseases or conditions previously unheard of or noted in only small numbers.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Texas Training Initiative for Emergency Response (T-Tier). (3-0). Credit 3. This course develops the knowledge, skills, and abilities needed to effectively respond to bioterrorism, infectious disease outbreaks, and other public health threats and emergencies in a multi-disciplinary approach. The course will focus on competencies paralleling the critical benchmark of emergency preparedness as identified by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, as well as to gain the knowledge, skills and abilities along with practice to protect the public's health. Roles of the many public health workers will be explored.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Laboratory Rotations. (0-9). Credit 3. subject: PHSC
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Biostatistics. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to basic statistical concepts and analytical methods; familiarization with statistical approaches used in pharmaceutical research and development; understanding the principles and development of skills for clinical research design, pre-clinical studies and clinical trials; understanding bio-statistical need for the result interpretation, introduction to evaluation of the medical literature and assessment of research reports and proposals; research terminologies, study design, statistical testing of data, investigator’s responsibilities in the ethical considerations of research; fundamentals of data sets and the evaluation of statistical results by employing examples of the clinical application of statistics; introduction to the methods used to conduct research in significant areas of pharmacy practice.

prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in MATH 151 or MATH 171 or equivalent; grade of C or better in ENGR 102; grade of C or better in PHYS 206 or concurrent enrollment; also taught at Galveston campus.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Experimental Physics and Engineering Lab II - Mechanics. (1-3). Credit 2. Cross-listed with ENGR 216.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 412.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Quantum Mechanics II. (3-0). Credit 3. Continuation of PHYS 412. Electron spin; addition of angular momenta; atomic structure; time dependent perturbations; collision theory; application of quantum mechanics to atomic, solid state, nuclear or high energy physics. Prerequisite: PHYS 412.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in PHYS 309.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Nuclear and Particle Physics. (3-0). Credit 3. Matter at the smallest scales and fundamental interactions between them; physics of atomic nuclei; physics of hadrons, quarks, leptons; fundamental strong and weak interactions; gauge bosons; state-of-the-art nuclear and particle physics; how knowledge was obtained; experimental confirmation of theoretical ideas; modern tools and instruments; foundations of nuclear technology; future perspectives. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHYS 309.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 304 and PHYS 412.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Physics of the Solid State. (3-0). Credit 3. A survey of solid state physics; an introduction to crystal structures and the physics of electrons, lattice vibrations and photons; applications to semiconductors; magnetism; superconductivity; physics of nanostructures; brief introduction to selected current topics in condensed matter physics. Prerequisites: PHYS 304 and PHYS 412.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in PHYS 309 or equivalent.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: High Energy Physics. (3-0). Credit 3. A broad spectrum of elementary particle physics along with historical and recent publication, covering symmetry in quarks and leptons, fundamental interactions, relativistic kinematics, Feynman diagrams, Dirac equation, cross-sections for particle reactions, unification of fundamental forces, accelerators and detectors and other current topics. Prerequisite: Grade of C or better in PHYS 309 or equivalent.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in PHYS 309 or PHYS 222.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Physics of Optoelectronic Devices. (3-0). Credit 3. Basic concepts of light-matter interaction, optics of semiconductors, nanostructures with quantum confinement and their interaction with light; physical principles of selected state-of-the-art optoelectronic devices; emerging concepts and technologies; examples of modern, state-of-the-art devices and emerging technologies. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in PHYS 309 or PHYS 222.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 327 or equivalent.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Physics Laboratory. (0-6). Credit 2. Experiments in nuclear, atomic, and molecular physics using modern instrumentation and equipment of current research. Prerequisite: PHYS 327 or equivalent.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 327 or equivalent.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Physics Laboratory. (0-6). Credit 2. Exercises of increasing complexity that utilize electronics-based techniques of experimental physics (lab-built amplifiers, synchronous detectors, tuned LRC circuits); measuring electron spin resonance and nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) absorption signals via marginal oscillator techniques; performing pre-set experiments on optical pumping of spin states in rubidium gas and on pulsed NMR. Prerequisite: PHYS 327 or equivalent.

Boundary-value problems in electrostatics; basic magnetostatics; multipoles; elementary treatment of ponderable media; Maxwell's equations for time-varying fields; energy and momentum of electromagnetic field; Poynting's theorem; gauge transformations. Prerequisites: PHYS 304 or equivalents; PHYS 615.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 412 or equivalent; MATH 311 and MATH 412 or equivalents; concurrent registration in PHYS 615.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Quantum Mechanics. (3-0). Credit 3. Schrodinger wave equation, bound states of simple systems, collision theory, representation and expansion theory, matrix formulation, perturbation theory. Prerequisites: PHYS 412 or equivalent; MATH 311 and MATH 412 or equivalents; concurrent registration in PHYS 615.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 408 and PHYS 412 or equivalents; PHYS 615.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Statistical Mechanics. (3-0). Credit 3. Classical statistical mechanics, Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution, and equipartition theorem; quantum statistical mechanics, Bose-Einstein distribution and Fermi-Dirac distribution; applications such as polyatomic gases, blackbody radiation, free electron model for metals, Debye model of vibrations in solids, ideal quantum mechanical gases and Bose-Einstein condensation; if time permits, phase transitions and nonequilibrium statistical mechanics. Prerequisites: PHYS 408 and PHYS 412 or equivalents; PHYS 615.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 603.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Electromagnetic Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. Continuation of PHYS 603. Propagation, reflection and refraction of electromagnetic waves; wave guides and cavities; interference and diffraction; simple radiating systems; dynamics of relativistic particles and fields; radiation by moving charges. Prerequisite: PHYS 603.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: MATH 311, MATH 407 and MATH 412 or equivalents.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Methods of Theoretical Physics I. (3-0). Credit 3. Orthogonal eigenfunctions with operator and matrix methods applied to solutions of the differential and integral equations of mathematical physics; contour integration, asymptotic expansions of Fourier transforms, the method of stationary phase and generalized functions applied to problems in quantum mechanics. Prerequisites: MATH 311, MATH 407 and MATH 412 or equivalents.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 615 or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Methods of Theoretical Physics II. (3-0). Credit 3. Group theory and its implementation in physical systems; finite groups, Lie groups and Lie algebras; representation theory, symmetries of regular objects, global aspects of Lie groups and classification of Lie algebras. Prerequisites: PHYS 615 or approval of instructor.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 606 and PHYS 607.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Physics of the Solid State. (3-0). Credit 3. Crystalline structure and symmetry operations; electronic properties in the free electron model with band effects included; lattice vibrations and phonons; thermal properties; additional topics selected by the instructor from: scattering of X-rays, electrons, and neutrons, electrical and thermal transport, magnetism, superconductivity, defects, semiconductor devices, dielectrics, optical properties. Prerequisites: PHYS 606 and PHYS 607.

Prerequisites: PHYS 408 and PHYS 412 or equivalents; knowledge of any programming language.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 606.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Quantum Mechanics. (3-0). Credit 3. Quantum dynamics, path integrals, quantum theory of scattering, relativistic quantum mechanics, second quantization, many-body quantum mechanics, quantum statistics, bosons and fermions, quantum electrodynamics, Bose-Einstein condensation. Prerequisites: PHYS 606.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 606.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Nuclear Physics. (3-0). Credit 3. Nucleon-nucleon interactions, properties of nuclear matter and atomic nuclei, nuclear reactions and astrophysics, hadron structure, nuclear matter under extreme conditions and topics of current interest. Prerequisite: PHYS 606.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 606, 615, and 625, or equivalent.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Theoretical Nuclear Physics. (3-0). Credit 3. Theoretical foundations of modern nuclear physics; quantum chromodynamics and properties; confinement; chiral symmetry and breaking; quark model and hadron structure; nuclear forces; many-body theory and effective field theory; fundamental symmetries; nuclear reactions and nuclear astrophysics; nuclear collisions and nuclear matter at high temperatures and densities; spectral functions and transport phenomena. Prerequisite: PHYS 606, 615, and 625, or equivalent.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 606.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Elementary Particle Physics. (3-0). Credit 3. Fundamentals of elementary particle physics; particle classification, symmetry principles, relativistic kinematics and quark models; basics of strong, electromagnetic and weak interactions. Prerequisite: PHYS 606.

prerequisite_text: PHYS 617 and PHYS 624.

Prerequisites: PHYS 617 and PHYS 624.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 601, PHYS 617 and PHYS 624.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 624.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 634.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Quantum Field Theory II. (3-0). Credit 3. Functional integrals; divergences, regularization and renormalization; non-abelian gauge theories; other topics of current interest. Prerequisite: PHYS 634.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 305 and PHYS 412; working knowledge of C or C++; or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_text: Quantum mechanics (PHYS 412 and PHYS 414 or PHYS 606 or equivalent).
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Physics of Optoelectronic Devices. (3-0). Credit 3. Overview of basic concepts: laser physics, optics of semiconductors, heterostructures with quantum confinement and their interaction with light; physical principles of state of the art optoelectronic devices; emerging concepts and technologies: integrated photonics, nanophotonics, plasmonics, metamaterials, terahertz optoelectronics, quantum information processing, etc. Prerequisites: Quantum mechanics (PHYS 412 and PHYS 414 or PHYS 606 or equivalent).

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 634 and PHYS 653; PHYS 647 recommended.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Superstring Theory I. (3-0). Credit 3. Basics of string theory, including bosonic string, conformal field theory, strings with worldsheet and space-time supersymmetry, as well as the higher dimensional extended objects called D-branes. Prerequisites: PHYS 634 and PHYS 653; PHYS 647 recommended.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 651; PHYS 647 recommended.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Superstring Theory II. (3-0). Credit 3. M-theory unification of superstring theories into a single eleven-dimensional theory; duality symmetries relating string theories; string geometry; Calabi-Yau manifolds and exceptional holonomy manifolds; flux compactifcations; black holes in string theory; AdS/CFT correspondence; string and M-theory cosmology. Prerequisites: PHYS 651; PHYS 647 recommended.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 634.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Introduction to Supersymmetry and Supergravity. (3-0). Credit 3. Core material on supersymmetric field theories and their coupling to supergravity theories. Prerequisite: PHYS 634.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 624 and PHYS 634.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: The Standard Model and Beyond. (3-0). Credit 3. The standard model of particle physics in detail; general principles of gauge theories, including spontaneous breaking and applications to Electro-Weak Interactions and Quantum Chromodynamics; extension of the standard model involving Grand Unified Theories (GUT), Supersymmetry (SUSY) and Supergravity (SUGRA). Prerequisites: PHYS 624 and PHYS 634.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 634 and PHYS 651.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: String Phenomenology. (3-0). Credit 3. Physical applications of string theory; rudiments of string theory; compactification of extreme dimensions in string theory; free-fermionic formulation; dualities, M-theory, intersection D-Branes, and D-Brane phenomenology; model building. Prerequisites: PHYS 634 and PHYS 651.

subject: PHYS
prerequisite_text: PHYS 408, PHYS 412, and PHYS 414, or equivalents.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Superfluidity and Superconductivity. (3-0). Credit 3. Basic properties of superconductors, superfluid 4He and superfluid 3He; Bose Einstein condensation, BCS theory and Ginzburg-Landau theory; methods of achieving low temperatures, with lab tours. Special topics include broken symmetry, neutron stars, ultra-cold atomic gases and tunneling in superconductors. Prerequisite: PHYS 408, PHYS 412, and PHYS 414, or equivalents.

prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Planning Methods II. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to a wide variety of methods and techniques of research, data collection and analysis, focusing on land use and infrastructure, analysis of land use demand and suitability, coordination of the planning process with public policy, and plan implementation. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PLAN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Geographical Information Systems in Landscape and Urban Planning. (2-3). Credit 3. Provides an understanding of GIS fundamentals; basic concepts, principles and functions; essential skills for applying GIS in various fields such as urban planning, landscape architecture, land development, environment studies, transportation and hazard management; based on learning through class projects. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

subject: PLAN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Geographical Information Systems in Landscape and Urban Planning. (2-3). Credit 3. Provides an understanding of GIS fundamentals; basic concepts, principles and functions; essential skills for applying GIS in various fields such as urban planning, landscape architecture, land development, environment studies, transportation and hazard management; based on learning through class projects. Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

subject: PLAN
prerequisite_text: PLAN 625.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Advanced GIS in Landscape Architecture and Urban Planning. (2-2). Credit 3. Continuation of GIS in Landscape Architecture and Urban Planning PLAN 625; topics include advanced spatial analysis technology: emphasis on urban planning, landscape architecture, land development, hazard management and related applications to issues. Prerequisite: PLAN 625.

subject: PLAN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Design for Active Living. (3-0). Credit 3. Understanding the forms and characteristics of the built environment and the influence on human behaviors, lifestyles and health; theoretical and empirical insights into the issues of physical activity, obesity and automobile dependency; focus on how changes in the built environment help address these issues. Prerequisite: Graduate classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with LAND 632.

subject: PLAN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Concepts in Ecological Planning and Design. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of ecological concepts and their potential applications in planning and design; introduction to landscape architects’ role as the steward of the earth; reinforcement of knowledge of nature and ecosystem; introduction to pioneering topics in the field of ecology; comprehensive explanations through reading materials, in-class discussions, and writing assignments; insights into real-world ecological planning and design endeavors via case studies and field trips. Prerequisites: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with LAND 635.

subject: PLAN
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Law and Legislation Related to Planning. (3-0). Credit 3. Legislative process and planning legislation; enabling legislation and legal tools of planner: zoning, subdivision ordinances, eminent domain, extraterritorial jurisdiction and other related planning instruments.

subject: PLAN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Planning for Community Sustainability and Resiliency. (3-0). Credit 3. Exploration of sustainability and resiliency in urban and community planning, with an emphasis on social vulnerability and environmental justice; analysis of interconnected socio-ecological systems, development of planning skills, evaluation of case studies, and engagement with stakeholders to address diverse needs. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: PLAN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Disaster Recovery Planning. (3-0). Credit 3.Exploration of the complexity, processes, and issues encountered in disaster recovery at the household, business, and community levels; examination and review of current disaster recovery research; and exploration of disaster recovery policies and recovery planning at Federal, State, and local levels. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Housing and Community. (3-0). Credit 3. subject: PLAN
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Plan Implementation. (3-0). Credit 3. subject: PLAN
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Applied Planning I. (1-6). Credit 3. Acquisition, analysis, and management of information pertaining to urban and regional planning in a case specific scenario; issue analysis; formulation of goals and objectives, and policies; consensus building; includes all tasks leading up to the preparation of an urban, regional or strategic plan.

subject: PLAN
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Site Planning. (2-4). Credit 3. subject: PLAN
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.

Prerequisite: Graduate classification.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Molecular Plant Virology. (1-0). Credit 1. Viruses are on the border between living and non-living biological entities. They are obligate intracellular parasites, and they infect all forms of living things from bacteria, algae and fungi to plants and animals. This course covers plant viruses focusing on viral structure, modes of reproduction, molecular biology of viral development and gene expression. This is a course in molecular aspects of virology. The course will explore basic and applied research in plant virology. There are three sections to the course which discuss a) plant virus taxonomy and evolution, b) virus replication and movement and c) virus-vector interactions. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Communication, Religion and the Arts. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Explores the study of art and religion as forms of communication, with attention to how visual and artistic expression conveys meaning across cultures and traditions. Surveys artistic and media practices in religious and secular contexts, considering how aesthetics mediate religious experience and shape public understanding. Examines the role of art in supporting, questioning and/or challenging religious and social perspectives. Focus on interpretation and critique and dialogue of artifacts across diverse traditions, including attention to issues of pluralism, inequality, power, class and/or representation. Includes engagement with perspectives that may be unfamiliar or challenging, reflecting the diversity of voices in contemporary public life. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Develops competence in interpreting and discussing art and religion across diverse cultural and historical contexts. Builds skills for engaging respectfully with differences in belief, practice and/or worldview. Strengthens intercultural awareness, critical thinking and creative communication skills, which can be applied to dialogue across divisions in civic, professional and interpersonal settings. Enhances understanding of how art and media shape public awareness of religion and contributes to broader conversations about meaning, identity and social conflict. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Clarifies how the study of art and religion in communication differs from devotional or confessional approaches. Expands understanding of religion as a cultural and communicative practice shaped by history, power and interpretation. Highlights how art functions not only to express belief but also to question, challenge or reframe religious ideas. Introduces perspectives that encourage critical analysis of how religion and art intersect with broader cultural, social and/or political contexts. Emphasizes reflection on pluralism and contested meanings, deepening awareness of how religion and art shape, and are shaped by, the wider human experience. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of communication, art and religion as interrelated cultural practices; exploration of how visual and artistic forms convey meaning within Christianity, Buddhism, Islam, secular humanism and other traditions; consideration of iconoclasm, pluralism and the role of art in shaping or challenging belief and practices; attention to aesthetics, power, inequality and representation in religious and secular contexts. Course materials may also engage with the profane or the obscene when relevant to understanding how religion, art and communication define, resist and/or reframe cultural boundaries. Content may include perspectives that are unfamiliar, contested or controversial, reflecting the diversity of ways art and religion intersect in public life. Cross-listed with COMM 257.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Introduction to Biblical Archaeology. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Introduces students to the archaeology and material culture of the Land of the Bible from the Epi-Paleolithic period through the first century A.D. The course examines the peoples, cities and societies of biblical times through material remains, integrating artifacts, iconography and texts to develop a holistic understanding of the ancient Near East. Students explore archaeological discoveries in relation to biblical narratives, including early agricultural communities, Canaanite city-states, Egyptian influence and Iron Age polities. The course also emphasizes the interpretation of archaeological evidence, historical context and the relationship of seafaring and trade to cultural development in the ancient biblical world. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues in biblical archaeology. TOPICS AND THEMES. Epi-Paleolithic period; Neolithic period; first agriculturists; Chalcolithic period; Early Bronze Age; Early Bronze IV; Middle Bronze Age I-II; Late Bronze Age; Egyptian influence in Canaan; maritime trade and seafaring; Iron Age I; Sea Peoples; Philistines; United Monarchy (Saul, David, Solomon); Divided Monarchy; Persian period; archaeology of biblical texts; material culture; urbanism; Canaanite city-states; fortifications; religious architecture; iconography; ceramics; metallurgy; inscriptions; settlement patterns; excavation techniques; interpretation of artifacts; relationship between archaeology and biblical narrative; cultural geography and human-environment interaction. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ANTH 317.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Anthropology of Religion. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Applies fundamental principles of cultural anthropology (the study of human variation and commonalities using a holistic mindset) to the analysis of religion. Examines the relationships connecting religion, culture, society and the individual through cross-cultural, theoretical analysis of religion as a cultural phenomenon. Investigates core questions regarding the existence and persistence of religion, analyzing how religious behavior manifests and connects with other cultural elements across diverse global settings. Includes analysis of religious practices, beliefs and institutions from a variety of cultures. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification; also taught at Galveston campus. prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Ancient Egypt II - Egypt in Decline. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Surveys the archaeology and history of ancient Egypt from the end of the New Kingdom through the Graeco-Roman period, focusing on the years 1185–30 BCE. Examines the decline of pharaonic power, the rise of foreign influences and the resilience of Egyptian society under Libyan, Nubian, Persian and Ptolemaic rule. Reviews the interplay between political, social and cultural dynamics, exploring Egyptian adaptations to Hellenistic dominance, while tracing continuity and change in art, religion, literature and urban development. Through lectures, readings and analyses of primary and secondary sources, students gain a humanistic understanding of Egyptian civilization during its final dynastic phases and develop skills in interpreting archaeological, textual and iconographic evidence. May incorporate topics that respond to current events, student interests or emerging issues pertaining to ancient Egypt. TOPICS AND THEMES. Decline of pharaonic authority; fragmentation of the Egyptian state; Libyan, Nubian and Persian interventions; internal political strife and social change; resilience of Egyptian cultural identity; Ptolemaic dynasty and Hellenistic influence; Cleopatra VII and the last Ptolemies; Alexandria as a cultural and economic center; Greco-Egyptian art, religion and literature; continuity and transformation of Egyptian traditions; interactions between foreign rulers and Egyptian elites; archaeological and textual methods for reconstructing late Egyptian history; humanistic approaches to interpreting material culture; synthesis of historical, artistic and archaeological evidence. Prerequisites: Completion of ANTH 436 or RELS 436 recommended but not required; junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ANTH 438.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Religious Communication. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. Examines the role of religious communication in shaping public life through speeches, sermons, debates, campaigns and/or social movements. Considers how religious language, symbols and/or narratives influence cultural identity, moral reasoning and/or collective action. Surveys diverse approaches to studying religious communication, from historical traditions to contemporary debates, highlighting how meaning is constructed, contested and transformed in religious discourse. Considers interpretations of religious communication from multiple perspectives, fostering critical thinking. Explores a diverse range of scholarly frameworks, theories and methods employed in the academic study of religion and religious communication. RELEVANCE AND APPLICATION. Strengthens transferable skills in critical thinking, interpretation and evaluation of persuasive messages in contexts ranging from personal dialogue to civic engagement. Enhances adaptability across diverse religious and cultural frameworks. Supports academic preparation for analyzing communication at the intersection of religion, culture and public life. Engages skills applicable to leadership, education, public study of advocacy and professional fields, when understanding religious perspectives and their influence is relevant. DEEPENING UNDERSTANDINGS. Considers how religious communication functions not only as a vehicle of belief but also as a force shaping history, politics and/or social change. Provides reflection on ways speeches, symbols and/or campaigns can both unite and divide, reinforcing traditions or sparking transformation. Provides frameworks for critical analysis of religious discourse from first-person and third-person perspectives. Highlights the interpretive challenges posed by pluralism, competing meanings and differing assumptions about authority, sacredness and public expression. TOPICS AND THEMES. May include study of religious speeches and sermons; debates over doctrine and belief; campaigns and movements shaped by religious rhetoric; analysis of religious symbolism and storytelling; exploration of the role of communication in sustaining or challenging religious traditions. Course materials may address diverse and sometimes controversial perspectives, reflecting the ways religious communication has influenced cultural identity, social conflict and civic life across history. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with COMM 480.

prerequisite_text: Graduate classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Wildlife Diseases. (3-0). Credit 3. This class provides an overview of diseases that affect wild mammals, birds, amphibians and reptiles. Emphasis is placed on diseases with population-level impacts to wildlife and those that are transmissible to humans or domestic animals and those found in Texas. For exams students should know common names of diseases, synonyms and the etiologic agent. They should be able to describe the agent and its basic history, its hosts and geographic distribution. Students need to be able to describe potential impact of specific diseases to wildlife population, if it is zoonotic and/or can be transmitted to/from domestic animals. They should be able to describe the signs of the disease, how it is transmitted, gross lesions, diagnostic criteria and prevention/control measures. Prerequisites: Graduate classification. Cross-listed with VTMI 631.

subject: SCSC
prerequisite_text: SCSC 301; knowledge of college-level algebra; graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Water in Soils and Plants. (3-0). Credit 3. Introduction to the physics of the soil-plant-atmosphere continuum; focus on soil, its physical properties, and their interactions with water and weather in terrestrial ecosystems; examination of processes including precipitation, rainfall interception, raindrop impact, infiltration, runoff, drainage, soil water storage, evaporation, transpiration, solar radiation partitioning, soil temperature, and heat transfer near the land surface; interactions of these processes with plant growth, solute transport, water quality, and greenhouse gas emissions are considered; quantitative analysis is emphasized with applications in soil and environmental science, agronomy, ecology, hydrology, and climatology. Prerequisites: SCSC 301; knowledge of college-level algebra; graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: SOPH

Sport has evolved into a global industry, with organizations increasingly expanding into international markets to access new consumers, revenue streams and development opportunities. Given this shift, current and aspiring sport industry professionals must understand various aspects of international sport business, such as economic and legal environments, governance structures, cultural differences, communication styles, management practices and the strategic challenges associated with operating in the global marketplace. prerequisite_text: Grade of C or better in CHEM 258 or CHEM 228; junior or senior classification; VIBS 277 or NRSC 277 recommended.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Developmental Neurotoxicology. (3-0). Credit 3. Effects of exposure to toxic substances on the developing nervous system; content to include mechanisms of toxicity of substances potentially devastating to the developing nervous system including lead, mercury and other heavy metals, alcohol, nicotine (smoking), pesticides, flame retardants, and others. Prerequisites: Grade of C or better in CHEM 258 or CHEM 228; junior or senior classification; VIBS 277 or NRSC 277 recommended. Cross-listed with NRSC 401.

subject: VIBS
prerequisite_text: BIMS 320 or equivalent; junior or senior classification.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Tumor Cell Biology and Carcinogenesis. (3-0) Credit 3. Principles of tumor biology; role of gene-environment interactions; molecular mechanisms regulating cancer initiation and progression; therapeutic treatment of cancer. Prerequisites: BIMS 320 or equivalent; junior or senior classification.

subject: VIBS
prerequisite_text: Senior classification; approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Endocrine Toxicology. (4-0). Credit 4. Impacts of endocrine toxicology on endocrine system; prevalence, environmental and occupational use and disposal of environmental endocrine disrupting chemicals (EDCs); structure, toxicokinetics and mechanism of action of EDCs; effects of EDCs on the development and function, disorders and diseases of the endocrine and reproductive organs. Prerequisites: Senior classification; approval of instructor.

subject: VIBS
prerequisite_text: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Methods in Vector-Borne Disease Ecology. (1-5). Credit 3. Methodological understanding of how vector-borne diseases are studied in the field and laboratory; hands-on exploration of the ecology disease systems in a one health framework; concepts of design, execution and presentation of research projects; outdoor field work and bio-safety level 2 laboratory. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification and approval of instructor. Cross-listed with ENTO 426.

subject: VIBS

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Biology of Mammalian Cells and Tissues. (3-3). Credit 4. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification in life sciences and interest in health related careers.

This course explores the principles and practices of cinematography and lighting in the context of contemporary virtual production. Students engage with both the practical craft of image, making and the critical analysis of cinematic form, investigating how light, lens and movement operate as expressive, technical and interpretive tools. Through film analysis, design exercises and virtual simulation with a 3D real-time game and simulation development system, the course bridges the traditions of studio cinematography with emerging digital workflows. The course emphasizes cinematography as a language of thought and emotion, uniting analytical insight with creative experimentation in both physical and virtual environments. Structured as a simulated professional production environment, students work in small teams to conceive, pitch, plan and execute a short narrative film utilizing the university’s LED volume stage (or equivalent virtual production technology). The semester functions as a single, continuous production cycle culminating in post-production finishing and professional delivery, resulting in a portfolio-ready short film that demonstrates technical fluency, creative leadership and team-based collaboration. Prerequisites: Grade C or better in VIST 200, VIST 325 or VIST 426; or approval of instructor.

subject: VIZA
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Virtual Cinematography and Lighting. (1-5). Credit 3. This course explores the principles and practices of cinematography and lighting in the context of contemporary virtual production. Students engage with both the practical craft of image, making and the critical analysis of cinematic form, investigating how light, lens and movement operate as expressive, technical and interpretive tools. Through film analysis, design exercises and virtual simulation with a 3D real-time game and simulation development system, the course bridges the traditions of studio cinematography with emerging digital workflows. Students learn how to construct, evaluate and refine cinematic imagery, translating aesthetic and narrative intention into visual and spatial composition. The course emphasizes cinematography as a language of thought and emotion, uniting analytical insight with creative experimentation in both physical and virtual environments. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

subject: VIZA
prerequisite_text: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: On Set Virtual Production. (1-5). Credit 3. This course serves as the culminating experience for the virtual production focus area, integrating prior coursework in digital storytelling, virtual cinematography, lighting and post-production. Structured as a simulated professional production environment, students work in small teams to conceive, pitch, plan and execute a short narrative film utilizing the university’s LED volume stage (or equivalent virtual production technology). The course emphasizes advanced project management, iterative content development (ICVFX/Unreal Engine asset creation), collaborative pre-visualization and the rigorous schedule of a physical virtual production shoot. The semester functions as a single, continuous production cycle culminating in post-production finishing and professional delivery, resulting in a portfolio-ready short film that demonstrates technical fluency, creative leadership and team-based collaboration. Prerequisites: Graduate classification or approval of instructor.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Wildlife Diseases. (3-0). Credit 3. This class provides an overview of diseases that affect wild mammals, birds, amphibians and reptiles. Emphasis is placed on diseases with population-level impacts to wildlife and those that are transmissible to humans or domestic animals and those found in Texas. For exams students should know common names of diseases, synonyms and the etiologic agent. They should be able to describe the agent and its basic history, its hosts and geographic distribution. Students need to be able to describe potential impact of specific diseases to wildlife population, if it is zoonotic and/or can be transmitted to/from domestic animals. They should be able to describe the signs of the disease, how it is transmitted, gross lesions, diagnostic criteria and prevention/control measures. Prerequisites: Graduate classification. prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Great Diseases of the World. (3-0). Credit 3. This course is designed to introduce you to major infectious diseases caused by viral, bacterial and parasitic pathogens that infect human beings, other mammals and sometimes insects. The lectures and assigned readings and videos focus on key historically important diseases, such as the plague, tuberculosis, cholera, influenza, yellow fever and HIV-AIDS, and recent emerging diseases, such as Ebola, Lassa Fever, COVID-19 and Monkey Pox. We will examine these diseases in depth, including their causes, historical impact, social and medical consequences, prevention and treatment. Prerequisite: Freshman or sophomore classification.

prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Wildlife Diseases. (3-0). Credit 3. This class provides an overview of diseases that affect wild mammals, birds, amphibians and reptiles. Emphasis is placed on diseases with population-level impacts to wildlife and those that are transmissible to humans or domestic animals and those found in Texas. For exams students should know common names of diseases, synonyms and the etiologic agent. They should be able to describe the agent and its basic history, its hosts and geographic distribution. Students need to be able to describe potential impact of specific diseases to wildlife population, if it is zoonotic and/or can be transmitted to/from domestic animals. They should be able to describe the signs of the disease, how it is transmitted, gross lesions, diagnostic criteria and prevention/control measures. Prerequisites: Junior or senior classification; approval of instructor. Cross-listed with RWFM 309.

This is an entry-level course designed to provide the students with an opportunity to gain an understanding of the basic features of the host defense system. The goal of this course is to familiarize the students with the mechanisms that are employed by the immune system to protect the host against infections and with the mechanisms that underlie aberrant immune responses including hypersensitivity reactions, autoimmune diseases and immune deficiency. The students are encouraged to engage in active discussions for easier assimilation and a comprehensive understanding of the subject matter. Prerequisite: Junior or senior classification.

subject: WGST
prerequisite_text: WGST 200.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Feminist Inquiry and Research Methods. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course is an interdisciplinary exploration of feminist research methods and inquiry in the humanities, social sciences and sciences. It explores ethical approaches to feminist research, feminist understandings of epistemology and feminist research design. TOPICS. Course may include but is not limited to discussions and readings about standpoint epistemology; poststructuralist, decolonial, feminist and queer approaches to research; and feminist science studies. Examples of feminist research discussed in class may focus on constructions of sex, gender, and sexuality, race/racism and other topics of contemporary relevance. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and instructor expertise and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisites: WGST 200.

subject: WGST
prerequisite_text: 6 hours in Women's and Gender Studies; senior classification or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Queer Theory. (3-0). Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. This course examines the field of queer theory as it emerged in the U.S. academy in the 1990s and grew and developed within and beyond U.S. borders in the early 21st century. The course includes scholarship on gender and sexual diversity and its overlaps with and divergences from feminist theories, while also highlighting the ways it functions as a critical practice that extends far beyond questions of gender and sexuality. Drawing on philosophy, literature, cultural studies and political theory, the course examines how “queer” operates as a challenge to systems of normalization — of identity, desire, embodiment and knowledge itself. The course considers foundational and contemporary texts in the field. TOPICS. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisites: 6 hours in Women's and Gender Studies; senior classification or approval of instructor. Cross-listed with SOCI 455.

subject: WGST
prerequisite_text: WGST 200 and junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
prerequisite_catalog_narrative: Senior Seminar. Credit 3. COURSE OVERVIEW. This capstone course for majors is an inquiry-based study of topics in women’s and gender studies. The course uses theories, analytic approaches and feminist and other methods in women’s and gender studies to investigate a topic of social and cultural significance. TOPICS. Topics will vary depending on the expertise of the instructor. The course includes development of research and writing skills such as forming research questions, practicing research methods and drafting and revising research-based writing. Instructors teaching this class will choose texts, assessments and approaches that represent current scholarship, instructor expertise, and satisfy course learning objectives. Prerequisites: WGST 200 and junior or senior classification; or approval of instructor.
